sections.title: Using SQL in a Programming Environment

blocks.text: Every statement you have written so far, you typed yourself. You opened a window, entered a `SELECT`, and read the rows that came back. That is a fine way to learn SQL and a fine way to answer a one-time question, but it is not how KimTay's business actually runs. Nobody at a pet supply distributor types a `SELECT` to look up a customer. A clerk clicks a name on a screen.
The screen is a program. Behind that program is the same database and the same SQL. This lesson is about the seam between the two: what changes when SQL stops being typed and starts being sent.
**Start with the data:** the first program sends a query to `CUSTOMER`. Read the complete table first, including the two rows assigned to rep 20.

blocks.caption: Source table: CUSTOMER — the data behind the first program query

blocks.text: The statement does not change

Start with the reassuring part. When the order-entry program shows every customer belonging to rep 20, it sends the database a statement you could have written in Module 5. Run it below. This is the exact text a program hands to the DBMS.

blocks.starter:
-- The statement a program sends when a clerk picks rep 20.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- The SELECT a stored procedure would wrap. Nothing about it changes because it
-- lives inside a procedure - only where the text is kept changes.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
-- In the procedure this literal is replaced by a parameter, which is the whole
-- point: one stored query answering the question for any rep.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Nothing new here. Read the two rows that come back and notice that they are ordinary result rows, not anything special because a program asked for them.

blocks.text: Two rows: Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. The DBMS does not know or care whether a person or a program asked. It parses the text, runs the query, and returns rows. That is the whole contract.
Embedded SQL

SQL embedded in a program is SQL written inside a host language such as Java, Python, PHP, or C#. The host language handles the screen, the buttons, and the loops. The SQL handles the data. The program opens a connection to the DBMS, sends statement text, and reads the rows that come back one at a time.
Here is the shape of it. The exact words differ by language, but the four moves are always the same.

# Host language (Python-style pseudocode). The SQL is the string in the middle.
# connect(): opens a session with the database server. The account named here is
#   the one whose privileges the SQL will run under - not the end user's.
conn = connect(database="kimtay", user="app_user", password="...")

# The SQL is just a string to the host language. These four lines are one
#   statement, split across lines only for readability.
sql = "SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE " \
      "FROM CUSTOMER " \

#   The ? is a PLACEHOLDER, not a value. Never paste the user's input into the
#   string - a placeholder is what keeps a typed value a value and stops it
#   being read as SQL, which is the whole defence against injection.
      "WHERE REP_NUM = ? " \
      "ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM"

# execute(): hands the statement and the values over separately. The database
#   parses the SQL once and then fills the placeholder with the value.
rows = conn.execute(sql, [rep_chosen_on_screen])

# The result comes back as a set of rows, and the host language walks it one row
#   at a time. This loop is the seam between the two languages: SQL thinks in
#   whole tables, the program thinks in single rows.
for row in rows:
    print(row.CUSTOMER_NUM, row.CUSTOMER_NAME, row.BALANCE)

items.title: Connect
items.body: The program opens a connection and identifies itself with a user name the DBA created. Privileges you learned in Module 7 apply to that user, not to the person at the keyboard.

items.title: Prepare
items.body: The program hands over statement text. The `?` is a placeholder, called a parameter or bind variable. The statement is compiled once with the hole still in it.

items.title: Execute
items.body: The program supplies a value for the placeholder and runs the statement. The DBMS substitutes the value safely, as data, and returns a result set.

items.title: Fetch
items.body: The program walks the result set one row at a time and does something with each. The rows arrive in the order the `ORDER BY` clause asked for; without that clause the DBMS promises no order at all, so a program that needs a particular order has to say so in the statement.

blocks.label: Why the placeholder matters
blocks.text: The program could have pasted the rep number straight into the string. It does not, for two reasons. The DBMS can reuse the compiled plan for every rep number instead of parsing new text each time, and a value supplied as a parameter can never be mistaken for SQL keywords. Pasted text can. That difference is the whole defense against SQL injection.
Why some logic lives in the database

Suppose KimTay has three programs that can change an item's price: the buyer's desktop tool, a nightly import from a supplier feed, and a small web page for corrections. Management wants every price change recorded, with the old price and the new one. You could write that logging code three times. Then somebody writes a fourth program, forgets, and the log has a hole in it.
The alternative is to put the rule where the data is. A stored procedure is a named block of SQL, saved in the database, that any program can call. Here is the MySQL form.

-- MySQL only. This sandbox runs SQLite, which has no CREATE PROCEDURE at all.
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE CUSTOMERS_OF_REP(IN REP_WANTED CHAR(2))
BEGIN
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    FROM CUSTOMER
    WHERE REP_NUM = REP_WANTED
    ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- MySQL only. Any program, in any language, can run this one line.
-- CALL: runs a stored procedure by name, passing its arguments in order. The
--   query text now lives in the database rather than in the application, so
--   every program shares one definition and one place to fix it.
CALL CUSTOMERS_OF_REP('20');

blocks.label: Engine label
blocks.text: `CREATE PROCEDURE`, cursors, PL/SQL and T-SQL are not supported by this sandbox in any form. Pasting the block above into a sandbox gives a syntax error on the word `PROCEDURE`. Read the two blocks above as MySQL, and do not expect output from them here.

What does run here is a trigger, which is the same idea with a different starting gun. A procedure runs when something calls it. A trigger runs when something changes the data, whether or not the program that made the change knows the trigger exists. That is exactly the property KimTay wants for price logging. One thing in the box below is borrowed from the next lesson: `DATE('now')` is how SQLite stamps a row with today's date, and Lesson 8-2c covers the date functions properly.

blocks.hint: One row comes back: CF21, 42.5, 44. The `UPDATE` at the bottom never mentions `PRICE_LOG`, yet the row is there, because `OLD` and `NEW` inside the trigger are the row before and after the change. The reset `UPDATE` near the top runs before the trigger exists, so it logs nothing and simply guarantees the same answer on a second Run.

cards.title: Belongs in the program
cards.body: Screen layout, which button was clicked, how to format a report, what to do when the user cancels. None of that is about the meaning of the data, and none of it should reach the database.

cards.title: Belongs in the database
cards.body: Rules that must hold no matter who is connecting: referential integrity, `CHECK` constraints, audit logging, privileges. Put a rule here once and every program inherits it, including the ones nobody has written yet.

items: A program sends the same SQL text you would type; the DBMS treats both the same way
Values from a screen travel as parameters, not as text pasted into the statement
Embedded SQL is four moves: connect, prepare, execute, fetch
A stored procedure is saved SQL that programs call by name; MySQL supports it, this sandbox does not
A trigger fires on a data change whether the program expects it or not, which is why integrity rules live in the database
A sandbox keeps its data between Runs, so a box that changes data has to put itself back to a known state first

blocks.text: A function takes one or more values and gives back one value. You have already used the aggregate functions from Module 5, which collapse many rows into one number. The functions in this lesson are different: they work on a single value at a time, so a query over the five rows of `ITEM` returns five results, one per row.

There is a catch, and it is the reason this lesson is longer than the others. The `SELECT` clause is standard across engines. The function library is not. Two databases that agree perfectly about `WHERE` and `GROUP BY` will disagree about how to get the year out of a date.

blocks.label: Read the engine label on every function
blocks.text: Everything in this section is marked. Functions that run in this sandbox appear in runnable blocks. Functions that are MySQL only appear in plain code blocks with a note, and each one is paired with the SQLite form that does run. Never assume a function is portable because it looks ordinary.
8-2a Character functions

Character functions reshape text. They do not change what is stored; they change what the query reports. That distinction matters, because it means you can clean up a value for a mailing label without editing the row.

blocks.caption: Character functions: MySQL compared with this sandbox
rows: LENGTH agrees on plain ASCII only; CHAR_LENGTH does not exist here

blocks.text: `UPPER` and `LOWER` are the plainest of the set. Add the two functions to the starter below and compare the report with the stored values.

blocks.starter:
-- Add an upper case name column and a lower case city column.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- UPPER and LOWER are ROW functions: they run once per row, so five rows in
-- means five rows out. Compare that with an aggregate, which returns one row.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM,
       UPPER(CUSTOMER_NAME) AS UPPER_NAME,
       -- The stored value is untouched; only the output is changed.
       LOWER(CITY) AS LOWER_CITY
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Wrap the column in the function and give the result a column name with `AS`. Access Pet Center becomes ACCESS PET CENTER, and Maple Grove becomes maple grove.

blocks.text: The useful place for `UPPER` is not the `SELECT` clause. It is the `WHERE` clause. Text comparison with `=` is case sensitive in this sandbox, so a search box that sends lower case text finds nothing. Run the starter first. Instead of a table you will get the message that the statement ran successfully and returned no rows, even though two customers are in Maple Grove.

blocks.starter:
-- Run this first. It matches nothing. Then fix it with UPPER.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CITY = 'maple grove'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY
FROM CUSTOMER
-- Applying UPPER to the COLUMN makes the comparison case-insensitive, so
-- 'Maple Grove' and 'MAPLE GROVE' both match. The cost is that the engine must
-- compute the function for every row before it can compare, which stops any
-- index on CITY from being used.
WHERE UPPER(CITY) = 'MAPLE GROVE'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Put both sides of the comparison in the same case: `UPPER(CITY)` on the left, a fully capitalized literal on the right. Capitalizing only one side still matches nothing. You should get customers 1120 and 1310.

blocks.label: A cost worth knowing
blocks.text: `WHERE UPPER(CITY) = 'MAPLE GROVE'` works, but wrapping a column in a function stops the DBMS from using an ordinary index on that column, because the index stores `Maple Grove`, not `MAPLE GROVE`. On four rows nobody notices. On four million rows a DBA does.

`SUBSTR` pulls a piece out of a string. It takes three arguments: the value, the starting position counted from 1, and how many characters to take. `LENGTH` counts the characters in a value. KimTay item numbers encode a category in the first two letters, so `SUBSTR` can expose that prefix as a column of its own.

blocks.starter:
-- Add the two-letter prefix of ITEM_ID and the length of DESCRIPTION.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION
FROM ITEM
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT ITEM_ID,
       -- SUBSTR(value, start, length): start counts from 1, not 0, so this takes
       -- the first two characters.
       SUBSTR(ITEM_ID, 1, 2) AS PREFIX,
       -- LENGTH counts characters in the value, ignoring the column's declared width.
       LENGTH(DESCRIPTION) AS NAME_LENGTH
FROM ITEM
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: `SUBSTR(ITEM_ID, 1, 2)` starts at character 1 and takes 2. AV07 gives AV. `LENGTH('Aviary Starter Cage')` is 19.

blocks.text: Because `LENGTH` returns a number, it works anywhere a number works, including `WHERE`. This is how you find values too long for a fixed-width label or a legacy screen.

blocks.starter:
-- Which item descriptions are longer than 20 characters?
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, LENGTH(DESCRIPTION) AS NAME_LENGTH
FROM ITEM
WHERE LENGTH(DESCRIPTION) > 20
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, LENGTH(DESCRIPTION) AS NAME_LENGTH
FROM ITEM
-- A function is legal in a WHERE clause as long as it is a ROW function - it
-- produces one value per row, so the condition can be tested row by row. An
-- aggregate here would be an error, because it needs the whole table first.
WHERE LENGTH(DESCRIPTION) > 20
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: Two rows come back: CF21 at 24 characters and GR15 at 25. Change 20 to 19 and FT88, at exactly 20, joins them.

blocks.text: `TRIM` removes blanks from both ends of a value and leaves the inside alone. Data that arrives from a spreadsheet or a supplier feed is full of stray blanks, and a value with a trailing space will not match a value without one. The seeded KimTay rows are clean, so the example below uses a literal to show the effect.

blocks.starter:
SELECT '[' || '  Maple Grove  ' || ']' AS RAW_VALUE,
       '[' || TRIM('  Maple Grove  ') || ']' AS TRIMMED_VALUE,
       LENGTH('  Maple Grove  ') AS BEFORE_LEN,
       LENGTH(TRIM('  Maple Grove  ')) AS AFTER_LEN;
blocks.solution:
-- Square brackets are just text, added so the spaces are visible on screen.
SELECT '[' || '  Maple Grove  ' || ']' AS RAW_VALUE,
       -- TRIM removes leading and trailing spaces, never the ones in the middle.
       '[' || TRIM('  Maple Grove  ') || ']' AS TRIMMED_VALUE,
       -- The two lengths are the proof: the spaces really were part of the value.
       LENGTH('  Maple Grove  ') AS BEFORE_LEN,
       LENGTH(TRIM('  Maple Grove  ')) AS AFTER_LEN;
blocks.hint: The brackets make the blanks visible. 15 characters before, 11 after. The space between Maple and Grove survives, because `TRIM` only touches the ends.

blocks.text: Character functions nest. The result of one is a value, so it can be the argument of the next. A three-letter rep code, capitalized, is one expression.

blocks.starter:
-- Build INITIALS (first letter of each name) and CODE (first three
-- letters of the last name, in capitals).
SELECT REP_NUM, FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT REP_NUM,
       -- Functions nest: SUBSTR takes the first letter of each name, and || glues
       -- the two results together into a pair of initials.
       SUBSTR(FIRST_NAME, 1, 1) || SUBSTR(LAST_NAME, 1, 1) AS INITIALS,
       -- Nested the other way round: take three characters, then upper-case the
       -- result. The inner function always runs first.
       UPPER(SUBSTR(LAST_NAME, 1, 3)) AS CODE
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.hint: Take one character from each name and join them with `||`, then wrap `SUBSTR(LAST_NAME, 1, 3)` in `UPPER`. Rep 20 gives VK and KAI.

blocks.text: 8-2b Number functions
Number functions are a shorter list and a calmer one. Two of them carry almost all the weight in business reporting: `ROUND` for money, and `ABS` for differences where the sign is noise.

blocks.caption: Number functions: MySQL compared with this sandbox

blocks.text: `ROUND(value, decimals)` rounds to the number of decimal places you name. Commission times rate is the classic case: the arithmetic can produce more decimal places than money has, and one of KimTay's three reps shows it clearly.

blocks.starter:
-- Add RAW_PAYOUT (COMMISSION * RATE) and PAYOUT (the same product
-- rounded to cents). Compare the two columns on rep 35.
SELECT REP_NUM, COMMISSION, RATE
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT REP_NUM, COMMISSION, RATE,
       -- The raw multiplication, showing every decimal place the engine produced.
       COMMISSION * RATE AS RAW_PAYOUT,
       -- ROUND(value, 2) cuts it to two decimals. Rounding at the point of
       -- DISPLAY is right; rounding money before you finish calculating is not.
       ROUND(COMMISSION * RATE, 2) AS PAYOUT
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.hint: Rep 35 is the one that matters. 39355 times 0.07 comes back as 2754.8500000000004, which is binary floating point showing through, and `ROUND(COMMISSION * RATE, 2)` reports it as 2754.85. Reps 20 and 65 were already clean at 1078 and 1188.2.

blocks.text: The same pattern gives you a line total on an invoice. Quantity times price is a number the database never stores, and rounding it at report time keeps the stored data untouched.

blocks.starter:
-- Add LINE_TOTAL: NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE, rounded to cents.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE
FROM INVOICE_LINE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE,
       -- The line total, computed per row and rounded to money.
       ROUND(NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE, 2) AS LINE_TOTAL
FROM INVOICE_LINE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: Invoice 50710 has two lines: 3 at 42.50 is 127.5, and 2 at 11.99 is 23.98. Whole amounts print without a trailing zero, so 2 at 42.50 on invoice 50711 shows as 85.

blocks.text: `ABS` returns a value without its sign. Reach for it when you want the size of a difference and the direction is either obvious or irrelevant. Credit headroom is a good example: `BALANCE - CREDIT_LIMIT` is negative for every KimTay customer, and the minus sign carries no information.

blocks.starter:
-- Add the raw difference and its absolute value.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME,
       -- The signed difference: negative for a customer who is under their limit.
       BALANCE - CREDIT_LIMIT AS DIFF,
       -- ABS drops the sign, giving the SIZE of the gap regardless of direction.
       -- Useful when you care how far apart two numbers are, not which is bigger.
       ABS(BALANCE - CREDIT_LIMIT) AS GAP
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Customer 1120 shows -3987.5 and 3987.5. Companion Care Clinic, with a zero balance, shows the widest gap at 10000.

blocks.text: An expression that works in `SELECT` works in `ORDER BY` too, so the same call ranks customers by available credit.

blocks.starter:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME,
       ABS(CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE) AS AVAILABLE
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY ABS(CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE) DESC;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME,
       ABS(CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE) AS AVAILABLE
FROM CUSTOMER
-- The expression is repeated here rather than reusing the alias. ORDER BY does
-- accept an alias, so ORDER BY AVAILABLE DESC would work too and read better.
ORDER BY ABS(CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE) DESC;
blocks.hint: Companion Care Clinic leads at 10000, and Whiskers and Wags Boutique trails at 1179.25.

blocks.text: Now the divergence. Rounding and chopping are not the same operation. MySQL has a function for chopping.

-- MySQL only. TRUNCATE does not exist in this sandbox and raises
-- "no such function: TRUNCATE".
-- SELECT: the stored price next to a version of it with the pennies cut off.
--   TRUNCATE(value, 0) chops at the decimal point - it does not round, so 64.99
--   becomes 64 rather than 65. Compare with ROUND if that matters.
SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE, TRUNCATE(PRICE, 0) AS WHOLE_DOLLARS

-- FROM: the table being read. Row functions like this one run once per row, so
--   five rows in means five rows out - unlike an aggregate.
FROM ITEM
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
The SQLite way to chop is to cast the value to an integer, which discards the fraction rather than rounding it. Run the comparison and look at AV07.

blocks.starter:
SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE,
       ROUND(PRICE, 0) AS ROUNDED,
       CAST(PRICE AS INTEGER) AS CHOPPED
FROM ITEM
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT ITEM_ID, PRICE,
       -- ROUND goes to the NEAREST whole number, so 64.99 becomes 65.
       ROUND(PRICE, 0) AS ROUNDED,
       -- CAST to INTEGER simply CHOPS the decimal part off, so 64.99 becomes 64.
       -- Two different answers from the same value - pick deliberately.
       CAST(PRICE AS INTEGER) AS CHOPPED
FROM ITEM
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: AV07 at 64.99 rounds to 65 but chops to 64. GR15 at 15.25 gives 15 either way. If a report must never overstate a price, those two columns are not interchangeable.

blocks.text: 8-2c Working with dates

Dates are where the two engines part company hardest. Not one of the MySQL date functions runs in this sandbox, and the SQLite forms do not do the same job in MySQL either: `strftime` and `julianday` do not exist there at all, and MySQL's own one-argument `DATE()` rejects the second argument that SQLite's date arithmetic depends on. Both engines answer the same questions; they use different words to ask.

blocks.label: The single biggest portability trap in this course
blocks.text: `CURDATE`, `NOW`, `YEAR` and `DATEDIFF` are MySQL. Typing any of them into this sandbox produces a no such function error. `DATE_ADD` fails even earlier, with a syntax error, because SQLite cannot parse `INTERVAL 30 DAY`. Learn both columns of the table below and always label which engine you are writing for.

blocks.caption: Date handling: MySQL compared with this sandbox

blocks.text:
-- MySQL only. Every function in this statement is unavailable in the
-- sandbox. The four sandboxes below do the same four jobs.
-- CURDATE(): today's date, taken from the server. It needs no column and no
--   arguments, so it returns the same value on every row.
SELECT CURDATE() AS TODAY,

--   YEAR(): pulls one part out of a date. There are matching MONTH() and DAY().
       YEAR(INVOICE_DATE) AS INVOICE_YEAR,

--   DATEDIFF(): the number of days between two dates, later one first.
       DATEDIFF(CURDATE(), INVOICE_DATE) AS DAYS_OLD,

--   DATE_ADD(): moves a date forward by an interval - the way to work out a due
--     date without doing arithmetic on the number by hand.
       DATE_ADD(INVOICE_DATE, INTERVAL 30 DAY) AS DUE_DATE

-- FROM: the table supplying INVOICE_DATE to all three date functions.
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;

Start with the clock. `DATE('now')` gives today as a date, and `DATETIME('now')` adds the time of day. Both read the clock on the machine running the database, so your result will not match the one printed in any hint here.

blocks.starter:
SELECT DATE('now') AS TODAY,
       DATETIME('now') AS RIGHT_NOW;
blocks.solution:
-- No FROM clause at all: these functions ask the server about itself, so there
-- is no table to read.
SELECT DATE('now') AS TODAY,
       -- DATETIME adds the time of day. DATE gives the calendar date alone.
       DATETIME('now') AS RIGHT_NOW;
blocks.hint: One row, two columns. `TODAY` is a plain YYYY-MM-DD value; `RIGHT_NOW` carries hours, minutes and seconds as well. The values change every time you run it.

blocks.text: To pull a piece out of a date, use `strftime` with a format code: `'%Y'` for the four-digit year, `'%m'` for the month, `'%d'` for the day. Combined codes are allowed, so `'%Y-%m'` gives a reporting period in one column. Note that `strftime` returns text, not a number.

blocks.starter:
-- Add the year, the month, and a combined YYYY-MM period column.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       -- strftime pulls a piece out of a date. %Y is the four-digit year.
       strftime('%Y', INVOICE_DATE) AS INVOICE_YEAR,
       -- %m is the two-digit month.
       strftime('%m', INVOICE_DATE) AS INVOICE_MONTH,
       -- Combining them gives a period label to group monthly reports by.
       strftime('%Y-%m', INVOICE_DATE) AS PERIOD
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.hint: All three KimTay invoices land in 2026, month 06, period 2026-06. The month comes back as the text 06, with the leading zero kept.

blocks.text: Date arithmetic uses `DATE(value, modifier)`. The modifier is a string such as `'+30 days'`, `'-1 month'`, or `'+1 year'`. KimTay's terms are net 30, so the due date of an invoice is thirty days past the invoice date. The starter below uses fifteen days; change it.

blocks.starter:
-- KimTay's terms are net 30, not net 15. Fix the modifier.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       DATE(INVOICE_DATE, '+15 days') AS DUE_DATE
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       -- DATE(value, modifier) shifts a date. The engine handles month ends and
       -- leap years, which is exactly why you never do this arithmetic by hand.
       DATE(INVOICE_DATE, '+30 days') AS DUE_DATE
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.hint: Change '+15 days' to '+30 days'. Invoice 50710, dated 2026-06-14, is then due 2026-07-14, and 50712 is due 2026-07-15.

blocks.text: The last question is how far apart two dates are. `julianday` converts a date to a running day number, and subtracting two of those numbers gives a difference in days. Run the starter alone first so the day numbers stop looking mysterious.

blocks.starter:
-- Step 1: see the raw day numbers.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS JULIAN
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       -- julianday turns a date into a single number of days, so subtracting two
       -- of them gives the days between. A fixed date is used here so the answer
       -- is the same whenever the query is run.
       julianday('2026-07-01') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS DAYS_OLD
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.hint: The raw numbers are around 2461205.5, which is meaningless on its own and exactly right as a difference. Subtract the invoice date from '2026-07-01' to get 17, 17 and 16 days.

blocks.label: When the fraction shows up
blocks.text: `julianday` returns a floating point value. Two plain dates are both stored at midday on the Julian scale, so their difference is a whole number and the sandbox simply prints 17. `julianday('now')` is different: it carries the time of day, so the same subtraction comes back as something like 50.10020332178101. Wrap the expression in `CAST(... AS INTEGER)` to get whole days, and remember that `CAST` chops rather than rounds, so an invoice 49.9 days old reports as 49.

blocks.starter:
-- Age each invoice against right now instead of a fixed date.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       julianday('now') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS RAW_DAYS,
       CAST(julianday('now') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS INTEGER) AS DAYS_OLD
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE_DATE,
       -- Against 'now' the result carries a fraction, because now includes a time
       -- of day and midnight on the invoice date does not.
       julianday('now') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS RAW_DAYS,
       -- CAST to INTEGER chops that fraction off, giving whole days elapsed.
       CAST(julianday('now') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE) AS INTEGER) AS DAYS_OLD
FROM INVOICE
ORDER BY INVOICE_NUM;
blocks.hint: `RAW_DAYS` comes back with a long fraction, because 'now' includes the clock time. `DAYS_OLD` is the same value with the fraction thrown away. Both columns grow by one every day, so your numbers will be larger than a classmate's from last week. Swap `'now'` for `'2026-07-01'` and the fraction disappears.

items: A single-row function returns one value per row; an aggregate returns one value per group
`UPPER`, `LOWER`, `SUBSTR` and `TRIM` behave the same in MySQL and here; `LENGTH` agrees too on plain ASCII, but MySQL counts bytes and wants `CHAR_LENGTH` for accented text
`ROUND` and `ABS` are portable; MySQL `TRUNCATE` is not, and `CAST(col AS INTEGER)` chops instead
`ROUND` rounds and `CAST` chops, and for 64.99 those give 65 and 64
Every MySQL date function has a SQLite counterpart and neither engine accepts the other's spelling
`DATE('now')`, `strftime('%Y', col)`, `julianday(a) - julianday(b)` and `DATE(col, '+30 days')` cover almost every date question you will be asked

blocks.text: Concatenation joins two or more character values into one. The database stores a rep's first name and last name in separate columns, which is correct: they are separate facts, and storing them apart is what lets you sort by last name. A mailing label wants them together. Concatenation is how a query delivers one without disturbing the other.
There are two spellings. `CONCAT` is a function and takes any number of arguments. The `||` operator joins exactly two values at a time, and you chain it for more. Both run in this sandbox.

blocks.starter:
-- Valerie Kaiser comes back as ValerieKaiser. Add the missing space.
SELECT REP_NUM,
       CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME) AS FULL_NAME
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT REP_NUM,
       -- CONCAT takes the pieces as arguments. It is the MySQL spelling, and
       -- SQLite has accepted it since version 3.44.
       CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME) AS FULL_NAME
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.hint: A space is a value like any other. Pass `' '` as a middle argument: `CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, ' ', LAST_NAME)`.

blocks.label: Concatenation
blocks.text: Joining character values end to end to form a single value. Nothing is added between them unless you supply it, which is why the separators, spaces, commas and dashes have to appear as literals in the expression.

The `||` operator does the same job in a form many people find easier to read, because the separators sit where they will appear in the output. Build a mailing line out of the three address columns of `REP`.

blocks.starter:
-- Build MAILING_LINE in the form: Maple Grove, OH 44601
SELECT REP_NUM, CITY, STATE, ZIP
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT REP_NUM,
       -- || is the STANDARD SQL concatenation operator, used between the pieces
       -- rather than around them. SQLite and Oracle both accept it; MySQL does
       -- not, which makes string joining one of the least portable corners of SQL.
       CITY || ', ' || STATE || ' ' || ZIP AS MAILING_LINE
FROM REP
ORDER BY REP_NUM;
blocks.hint: Chain the operator: column, separator, column, separator, column. The comma and the spaces are literals in quotes. Reps 20 and 35 both give Maple Grove, OH 44601.

blocks.text: For a longer label, `CONCAT` usually reads better than a chain of four or five operators, because the separators are arguments in a list rather than punctuation between operators.

blocks.starter:
-- Build a one-line mailing label per customer:
-- Access Pet Center, 215 Foster Ave., Maple Grove OH 44601
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, STREET, CITY, STATE, ZIP
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM,
       -- One CONCAT call can take as many arguments as you need. The literal
       -- commas and spaces are supplied as their own arguments.
       CONCAT(CUSTOMER_NAME, ', ', STREET, ', ', CITY, ' ', STATE, ' ', ZIP) AS MAILING_LABEL
FROM CUSTOMER
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Nine arguments in all: the five columns and the four separators between them. Watch the comma after the street but the plain space before the state.

blocks.text: The null problem

Here is the part that costs people real time. Concatenating a value with null does not do the harmless thing you might expect, and what it does depends on the engine and on the spelling you chose. `COALESCE(value, replacement)` is the tool for the job: it hands back the first argument unless that argument is null, in which case it hands back the second. Run this and read all three columns.

blocks.solution:
-- The three ways a null behaves when you join strings, side by side.
-- CONCAT treats a null as an empty string, so the label survives.
SELECT CONCAT('Rep: ', NULL) AS CONCAT_RESULT,
       -- || is stricter: a null anywhere makes the WHOLE result null, so the
       -- text you wrote disappears too.
       'Rep: ' || NULL AS PIPE_RESULT,
       -- COALESCE returns its first argument that is not null, which is how you
       -- substitute a readable stand-in before the null can spread.
       'Rep: ' || COALESCE(NULL, 'unassigned') AS SAFE_RESULT;
blocks.hint: `CONCAT_RESULT` is the text Rep: with the null skipped. `PIPE_RESULT` is null, and this sandbox prints a null cell as the word NULL, so you will see NULL there rather than a blank. `SAFE_RESULT` is Rep: unassigned, because `COALESCE` replaced the null before the join happened.

blocks.caption: What happens when a null joins the expression
rows: The same call gives opposite answers in the two engines
NULL, but only because || means OR there unless PIPES_AS_CONCAT is set
One null makes the entire pipe expression null here
Handle the null yourself and both engines agree

blocks.label: Three engines, three answers
blocks.text: MySQL `CONCAT` returns null if any argument is null; this sandbox skips the null and returns the rest. In MySQL, `||` is the logical OR operator by default, not concatenation at all. Oracle does use `||` for concatenation the way this sandbox does, but Oracle treats a null as an empty string, so there the label survives instead of going null. Never carry a concatenation expression between engines without testing it.

None of the seeded KimTay rows contain a null, so where does a real null come from? From a query. Module 6 showed that an outer join manufactures nulls for the unmatched side, and Companion Care Clinic has no invoice. Run this and watch that one customer lose its whole label.

blocks.starter:
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
       C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || I.INVOICE_NUM AS PIPE_LABEL,
       CONCAT(C.CUSTOMER_NAME, ' / ', I.INVOICE_NUM) AS CONCAT_LABEL,
       C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || COALESCE(I.INVOICE_NUM, 'no invoice') AS SAFE_LABEL
FROM CUSTOMER C
LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
ORDER BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
       -- For the unmatched customer the LEFT JOIN supplies a null invoice number,
       -- and || turns the entire label null.
       C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || I.INVOICE_NUM AS PIPE_LABEL,
       -- CONCAT keeps the name and simply leaves a gap where the null was.
       CONCAT(C.CUSTOMER_NAME, ' / ', I.INVOICE_NUM) AS CONCAT_LABEL,
       -- COALESCE is the version to actually ship: it says what the gap means.
       C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || COALESCE(I.INVOICE_NUM, 'no invoice') AS SAFE_LABEL
FROM CUSTOMER C
-- LEFT JOIN keeps the customer with no invoice, which is what creates the null.
LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
ORDER BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Four rows. Three customers look identical across all three label columns. Companion Care Clinic does not: `PIPE_LABEL` prints as NULL, `CONCAT_LABEL` trails off after the slash, and only `SAFE_LABEL` says what is going on.

blocks.text: The lesson is not that concatenation is dangerous. It is that a label built from a column that might be null needs a decision from you about what the null should read as. `COALESCE` is where you record that decision, and it is portable across every engine in this course.

items: `CONCAT(a, ' ', b)` and `a || ' ' || b` both join values in this sandbox
Separators are literals you supply; nothing appears between values on its own
In this sandbox `||` returns null if either side is null, while `CONCAT` skips the null
MySQL `CONCAT` returns null instead, and MySQL reads `||` as OR by default
A null result prints in this sandbox as the word NULL, which is the engine telling you there is no value, not a blank label
Wrap any nullable column in `COALESCE` before concatenating and both engines produce the same label
Outer joins are the usual source of nulls in otherwise complete data, as Companion Care Clinic shows

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: SQL inside a program

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's order-entry screen
questions.stem: A clerk opens KimTay's order-entry program and picks rep 20 from a dropdown. The screen fills with Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. What did the program hand to the DBMS?
options: A special program-only command that bypasses SQL and reads the stored table files directly
A compiled binary copy of the CUSTOMER table that the program decodes on its own
The same SELECT statement you would type by hand, with the rep number supplied as a parameter
A request for every row in CUSTOMER, which the program then filtered down in memory
optionNotes: There is no bypass; every client, program or person, communicates with the DBMS in SQL.
Programs receive result rows over a connection, not a decoded copy of the stored table.
Correct: the program builds the same SELECT you know and supplies a value for the placeholder.
Filtering in the program instead of in the WHERE clause would drag every customer row across the connection for nothing.
questions.takeaway: A program sends the same SQL text you would type; only the way values are supplied changes.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's price-change rule
questions.stem: Three different KimTay programs can change an item's price, and every change must be recorded with its old and new value. Why would the DBA put that rule in the database rather than in each program?
options: One copy of the rule runs no matter which program makes the change, so it cannot be skipped
Database code always runs faster than application code, whatever work the code is doing
SQL inside a procedure uses a different and more powerful language than the SQL you type
Keeping the rule in the database removes the need to grant users any privileges at all
optionNotes: Correct: logic stored in the database applies to every connection, including programs written later.
Speed depends on the work being done; the reason here is one enforced copy of the rule, not raw speed.
A procedure holds the same SQL statements plus control flow; the SELECT and INSERT are unchanged.
Privileges are a separate mechanism, and procedures do not replace GRANT and REVOKE.
questions.takeaway: Rules that must hold for every program belong in the database, where no program can forget them.

questions.scenarioTitle: Running the price-log box twice
questions.stem: A student runs the trigger sandbox, sees CF21 logged from 42.5 to 44, and presses Run again without pressing Reset. Why does the box begin by setting CF21's price back to 42.50?
options: Because the sandbox reloads the seeded data before every Run, so the line is only a comment in effect
Because CREATE TRIGGER refuses to run unless the table it watches has its original values
Because the sandbox keeps the data as you left it, so without the reset the second Run would log 44 changing to 44
Because DROP TABLE PRICE_LOG also rolls the ITEM table back, and the UPDATE undoes that rollback
optionNotes: The sandbox reseeds only when you press Reset or reload the page, not on every Run.
CREATE TRIGGER does not inspect or care about the data already in the table.
Correct: the first Run left PRICE at 44.00, so OLD.PRICE would be 44 and the demonstration would collapse.
DROP TABLE removes PRICE_LOG only; it has no effect on ITEM at all.
questions.takeaway: A sandbox that changes data keeps those changes between Runs, so a repeatable box has to reset its own starting state.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: functions and engine differences

questions.scenarioTitle: Searching for Maple Grove
questions.stem: A search box sends `WHERE CITY = 'maple grove'` to the sandbox. KimTay stores the city as `Maple Grove`, and the query returns no rows at all. Which change fixes the match in both MySQL and this sandbox?
options: Compare `LOWER(CITY)` to the literal `'MAPLE GROVE'`, since putting one side through a case function is enough
Compare `UPPER(CITY)` to the literal `'MAPLE GROVE'` so both sides use the same case
Replace the equals sign with `LIKE`, which ignores letter case in every engine and column
Wrap the column in `LENGTH(CITY)` so the comparison no longer depends on case
optionNotes: Lowering the column while leaving the literal capitalized still compares 'maple grove' to 'MAPLE GROVE', so it matches nothing.
Correct: UPPER on the column plus a capitalized literal puts both sides in the same case.
LIKE's case behavior comes from collation settings that differ by engine and by column, so it is not a dependable fix.
LENGTH counts characters, so two different words of equal length would compare as equal.
questions.takeaway: Force both sides of a text comparison into the same case rather than trusting the engine's default.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's whole-dollar inventory sheet
questions.stem: An inventory sheet must show each `ITEM` price in whole dollars with the cents dropped, never rounded up. AV07 is priced at 64.99. Which statement is true in this sandbox?
options: `ROUND(PRICE, 0)` discards the cents without rounding, so it already satisfies the rule
`TRUNCATE(PRICE, 0)` runs here and is the portable choice across both engines
SQLite offers no control over decimal places, so the program has to format the number
`ROUND` rounds rather than chops, so chopping needs MySQL `TRUNCATE` or `CAST(PRICE AS INTEGER)` here
optionNotes: ROUND moves to the nearest value, turning 64.99 into 65 and overstating the price.
TRUNCATE is a MySQL function; this sandbox answers with a no such function error.
ROUND and CAST both control decimals here, so the work does not have to leave the database.
Correct: ROUND rounds, and chopping requires MySQL TRUNCATE or a SQLite CAST to an integer.
questions.takeaway: Rounding and chopping are different operations, and the chopping spelling differs by engine.

questions.scenarioTitle: Aging KimTay invoice 50710
questions.stem: Invoice 50710 is dated 2026-06-14, and a collections report needs its age in days as of 2026-07-01. Which expression produces 17 in this sandbox?
options: `julianday('2026-07-01') - julianday(INVOICE_DATE)`, which subtracts two running day numbers
`DATEDIFF('2026-07-01', INVOICE_DATE)`, the standard day-difference function in every engine
`'2026-07-01' - INVOICE_DATE`, because the engine understands date subtraction directly
`strftime('%d', '2026-07-01') - strftime('%d', INVOICE_DATE)`, subtracting the two day numbers
optionNotes: Correct: julianday turns each date into a day number, and the difference is a count of days.
DATEDIFF is MySQL only; the sandbox reports no such function for it.
Dates are stored as text here, so subtracting them gives 0, not a number of days.
This subtracts day-of-month values only. Here it gives 1 minus 14, or -13, and it breaks whenever the two dates fall in different months.
questions.takeaway: Day differences come from julianday here and from DATEDIFF in MySQL, and the two are never interchangeable.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's June sales summary
questions.stem: A summary groups KimTay invoices by the year they were written. Which expression returns 2026 for every row of `INVOICE` in this sandbox?
options: `YEAR(INVOICE_DATE)`, since YEAR is part of the SQL standard and available everywhere
`DATE(INVOICE_DATE, 'year')`, which asks the DATE function for the year portion
`strftime('%Y', INVOICE_DATE)`, which formats the date and returns the four-digit year
`SUBSTRING(INVOICE_DATE, 5, 4)`, which reads the year out of the stored text
optionNotes: YEAR is a MySQL function and raises a no such function error in this sandbox.
The second argument of DATE is a modifier such as '+30 days'. 'year' is not one, so the call returns NULL for every row rather than reporting an error.
Correct: strftime with the '%Y' code returns 2026 as text for all three invoices.
The year sits in positions 1 through 4 of a YYYY-MM-DD value, so starting at 5 returns '-06-' instead.
questions.takeaway: Use strftime with a format code to pull any piece out of a date in this sandbox.

questions.scenarioTitle: Rep 20's name on a mailing label
questions.stem: A label for rep 20 should read `Valerie Kaiser`, but `CONCAT(FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME)` returns `ValerieKaiser`. What went wrong?
options: CONCAT accepts only two arguments, so the third value was silently dropped from the result
The FIRST_NAME column was stored with its trailing blanks removed by the DBMS
CONCAT joined the columns in the wrong order, which removed the space between them
Nothing appears between two concatenated values unless the expression supplies it as a literal
optionNotes: CONCAT accepts many arguments here; the call in the stem passed only two of them.
No blanks were stored to begin with, and TRIM was never applied to this expression.
The order is correct; the names appear in the order they were listed, with nothing between them.
Correct: add `' '` as a middle argument, or write `FIRST_NAME || ' ' || LAST_NAME`.
questions.takeaway: Separators in a concatenated value are literals you write out, never something the engine adds.

questions.scenarioTitle: Labeling KimTay customers with their invoice
questions.stem: A `LEFT JOIN` from `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE` builds the label `C.CUSTOMER_NAME || ' / ' || I.INVOICE_NUM`. Three labels read correctly and Companion Care Clinic's cell reads NULL. Why?
options: The customer name for 1310 is missing, so there is nothing on the left of the expression
Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so INVOICE_NUM is null and the whole pipe expression is null
The LEFT JOIN dropped customer 1310 entirely, which is why no label appeared for it
The zero balance on customer 1310 made the concatenation evaluate to an empty string
optionNotes: The name is present; the SELECT shows CUSTOMER_NAME correctly in the neighboring column.
Correct: one null anywhere in a || chain makes the entire result null, which this sandbox displays as the word NULL.
A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, which is exactly why the unmatched row is visible at all.
BALANCE takes no part in this expression, and a zero balance is a value rather than a null.
questions.takeaway: An outer join manufactures nulls, and a null anywhere in a || chain wipes out the whole label.

questions.scenarioTitle: Moving KimTay's label query to MySQL
questions.stem: A label expression written here as `CONCAT(CUSTOMER_NAME, ' / ', INVOICE_NUM)` is moved to MySQL, where some invoice numbers come back null. What should you expect?
options: MySQL produces the identical output, because CONCAT is defined the same way in both engines
MySQL raises an error on the null argument and refuses to run the statement
MySQL returns null for those rows, because its CONCAT is null if any argument is null
MySQL substitutes an empty string automatically, which is what this sandbox does as well
optionNotes: The two engines disagree on this exact point, which is why the expression is not portable as written.
Nulls are legal arguments in both engines; neither raises an error for one.
Correct: MySQL CONCAT returns null on any null argument, while this sandbox skips it and returns the rest.
This sandbox does skip the null, but MySQL does not, so the outputs differ.
questions.takeaway: Wrap nullable columns in COALESCE before concatenating and the expression behaves the same on every engine.

matchers.heading: Match the MySQL date call to the sandbox form
matchers.prompt: KimTay's reporting queries were written against MySQL and have to run in this SQLite sandbox. Drop each MySQL expression on the SQLite form that does the same job here.

cards.text: CURDATE()
cards.why: CURDATE returns today with no time attached, which is what DATE('now') gives here.

cards.text: CURRENT_DATE()
cards.why: CURRENT_DATE() is MySQL's synonym for CURDATE(), so it lands on DATE('now') as well.

cards.text: NOW()
cards.why: NOW carries hours, minutes and seconds, so the match is DATETIME('now'), not DATE('now').

cards.text: SYSDATE()
cards.why: SYSDATE also returns a date and time value, so it lands on DATETIME('now') too.

cards.text: YEAR(INVOICE_DATE)
cards.why: YEAR extracts the four-digit year, which strftime does here with the '%Y' format code.

cards.text: EXTRACT(YEAR FROM INVOICE_DATE)
cards.why: EXTRACT is the ANSI spelling MySQL also accepts for the same extraction, so it maps to strftime('%Y', col) too.

cards.text: DATEDIFF('2026-07-01', INVOICE_DATE)
cards.why: DATEDIFF counts days between two dates, which you get here by subtracting two julianday values.

cards.text: DATE_ADD(INVOICE_DATE, INTERVAL 30 DAY)
cards.why: DATE_ADD shifts a date forward, which the modifier '+30 days' does inside SQLite's DATE function.

blocks.text: A stored procedure is a named block of SQL that lives inside the database itself. You write it once, the server stores it, and from then on anyone with permission runs it by name. The SQL does not sit in a text file on somebody's laptop, and it is not pasted into four different application screens that slowly drift apart. It lives next to the data it operates on.

blocks.label: Engine note - read this once
blocks.text: Nothing in 8-4, 8-5, or 8-6 is a sandbox exercise, so there is no Run button in these three sections and that is expected. The sandbox is SQLite, and SQLite has no stored procedures at all: no `CREATE PROCEDURE`, no `DELIMITER`, no `DECLARE`, no `CALL`, and no `GRANT`. Everything below is MySQL, shown in plain code blocks for you to run in MySQL Workbench or the `mysql` client against the KimTay database. One caution: the two deliberate counter-examples in 8-6, a bare `UPDATE` and a bare `DELETE` with no `WHERE` clause, are ordinary SQL that any engine will happily run. That is exactly why they are dangerous, and exactly why they are labelled. Do not run them against data you care about.
Why put SQL in the database
You already know how to write every statement a procedure contains. The question is where those statements should live. Moving them into the database buys you several things at once.

items: One correct copy. The rule for adjusting a balance exists in exactly one place, so fixing it fixes it everywhere.
Reuse by name. A report writer, a web application, and a nightly job can all issue the same `CALL` instead of each rewriting the query.
Fewer round trips. Five statements sent one at a time is five conversations with the server; one `CALL` is one.
A safety boundary. An account can be allowed to run a procedure without being allowed to run raw `DELETE` against the table. 8-6 shows how that is arranged and what it depends on.
A home for the hard parts. The tricky join, the exact `WHERE` clause, the error handling: written once by whoever knows the schema best.

blocks.text: What a procedure looks like

Start with the smallest useful example. This one takes no parameters and reports how many sales reps KimTay has. The `DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS` line is there so you can edit and re-run the script as often as you like.

-- DELIMITER //: switch the statement terminator so the semicolons inside the
--   procedure are not mistaken for the end of it.
DELIMITER //

-- DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS: makes the script re-runnable. Without it, the second
--   run fails because the procedure already exists.
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHOW_REP_COUNT //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the simplest possible one - empty parentheses mean it takes
--   no parameters at all.
CREATE PROCEDURE SHOW_REP_COUNT()

-- BEGIN ... END wrap the body.
BEGIN

    -- One ordinary statement. Its result is returned to the caller.
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS REP_COUNT FROM REP;
END //

-- Restore the normal semicolon.
DELIMITER ;

Four parts matter. `CREATE PROCEDURE SHOW_REP_COUNT()` names the procedure and gives it an empty parameter list. `BEGIN` and `END` bracket the body. Inside the body, ordinary SQL statements each end with a semicolon. And the whole thing is wrapped in a pair of `DELIMITER` commands, which is the part that surprises everyone the first time.

blocks.label: DELIMITER
blocks.text: `DELIMITER` is not SQL and the server never sees it. It is an instruction to your client program telling it which characters mark the end of a statement. Normally that is the semicolon. But a procedure body is full of semicolons, so a client using the default rule chops `CREATE PROCEDURE` into pieces and sends the first fragment on its own, which is a syntax error. `DELIMITER //` changes the rule to two slashes, so the client sends the entire `CREATE PROCEDURE ... END` as one statement. `DELIMITER ;` puts the rule back.

Any character sequence that does not appear in your code will work, and `//` and `$$` are the two you will see most often. Avoid the backslash, which MySQL treats as an escape character, and avoid a sequence that is itself an operator, such as a single `|`. Whichever one you pick, remember two things: the statements between the two `DELIMITER` commands must end with that sequence instead of a semicolon, and you must set the delimiter back to `;` at the end or every later statement in your session will look wrong to the client.
Running the procedure takes one word:

The result is a single row with a single column, `REP_COUNT`, holding 3: Kaiser, Hull, and Perez. A procedure whose body ends in a bare `SELECT` sends that result set straight back to whoever called it, exactly as if you had typed the `SELECT` yourself.
Parameters: IN, OUT, and INOUT

A procedure with no parameters can only ever do one thing. Parameters are how a caller says which customer, which item, how much. Each parameter is declared with a mode, a name, and a data type, in that order. Leave the mode off and MySQL assumes `IN`.

blocks.caption: The three parameter modes
rows: Caller to procedure. The body may change its own copy, but the caller never sees that change.
Procedure to caller. MySQL sets the value to NULL as the procedure starts, whatever the caller passed.
Both directions. The body sees the value the caller supplied and hands back whatever it leaves there.

blocks.text: An `OUT` or `INOUT` argument has to be something that can be written to, so the caller passes a session variable such as `@balance`, never a literal. Passing `250.00` where an `OUT` parameter is expected is an error.

blocks.label: Never name a parameter after a column
blocks.text: Inside a procedure body, when a name could mean either a declared parameter or a column, MySQL resolves it as the parameter. Name a parameter `REP_NUM` and the condition `WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM` becomes the parameter compared with itself, which is true for every row in the table. The prefixes used throughout these sections - `i_` for `IN`, `o_` for `OUT`, `io_` for `INOUT`, `v_` for a local variable - exist to make that collision impossible.
Here is the mistake made concrete, so that you recognize it when it happens to you:

-- DELIMITER //: as always, so inner semicolons are safe.
DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS BAD_REP_NAME //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one is broken on purpose - watch the parameter name.
CREATE PROCEDURE BAD_REP_NAME(

    -- IN parameter named REP_NUM, which is ALSO the name of a column in REP.
    --   That collision is the bug.
    IN  REP_NUM     CHAR(2),

    -- OUT parameter: a value the procedure hands back to the caller.
    OUT o_last_name VARCHAR(20))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO: instead of returning a result set, the value found is put
    --   into a variable. It expects exactly one row.
    SELECT LAST_NAME
    INTO   o_last_name
    FROM   REP

    -- BROKEN. Both sides of this comparison are read as the COLUMN REP_NUM, so
    --   the condition says "where the column equals itself" - true for every row.
    --   That is why parameters are conventionally prefixed i_ or p_: the prefix
    --   makes a collision like this impossible.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = REP_NUM;
END //

DELIMITER ;

-- CALL: passing the rep number and a session variable to receive the answer.
--   Because of the name collision, the WHERE clause matched every rep, so the
--   procedure returns whichever last name the engine happened to reach - not
--   necessarily rep 35's.
CALL BAD_REP_NAME('35', @last);

The procedure is created without complaint. The call fails with ERROR 1172 (42000): Result consisted of more than one row, because the `WHERE` clause matched all three rep rows, Kaiser, Hull, and Perez. Notice how the error blames the wrong thing: it reports too many rows, not the naming collision that produced them. Rename the parameter to `i_rep_num` and the procedure behaves.
8-4a Retrieving a single row

The most common job for a procedure is to look one thing up and hand it back. `SELECT ... INTO` does that: it runs an ordinary query, then copies each selected column into the variable named in the matching position of the `INTO` list. One column or several, it is built for a query that returns exactly one row. Zero rows and it assigns nothing; two or more rows and it raises an error. Both of those cases are the subject of 8-5.

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DISP_REP_NAME //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the fixed version of the previous example.
CREATE PROCEDURE DISP_REP_NAME(

    -- The i_ prefix keeps the parameter name distinct from the column name.
    IN  i_rep_num    CHAR(2),

    -- Two OUT parameters: a procedure may hand back as many values as you like.
    OUT o_last_name  VARCHAR(20),
    OUT o_first_name VARCHAR(20))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO with two columns and two variables. They are matched by
    --   position, so the order of the two lists has to agree.
    SELECT LAST_NAME, FIRST_NAME
    INTO   o_last_name, o_first_name
    FROM   REP

    -- Now the comparison is genuinely column against parameter.
    WHERE  REP_NUM = i_rep_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Because `REP_NUM` is the primary key of `REP`, that `WHERE` clause can match at most one row, which is what makes `SELECT ... INTO` the right tool here. Two columns are selected and two variables are listed, in the same order. Call it, then read the session variables the same way you read any expression:

The result is one row: `LAST_NAME` is Hull and `FIRST_NAME` is Richard. The `CALL` itself displays nothing. The procedure put its answers into `@last` and `@first`, and the `SELECT` that follows is what shows them.

blocks.text: Local variables and a computed answer

Sometimes the value you want is not stored anywhere and has to be worked out. A local variable gives the body somewhere to hold an intermediate result. Declare it with `DECLARE`, give it a type, and optionally a `DEFAULT`. Every `DECLARE` has to appear at the top of the block, before the first executable statement, and a local variable declared without a `DEFAULT` starts each call as NULL. Assign to it with `SET`, or by naming it in an `INTO` list.
KimTay's credit department keeps asking how much room a customer has left. That is `CREDIT_LIMIT` minus `BALANCE`, and no column holds it:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one computes something rather than just fetching it.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CREDIT_AVAILABLE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_available    DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE: a LOCAL variable, visible only inside this procedure and gone the
    --   moment it ends. Every DECLARE must come before the first real statement
    --   of the body. Note there is no @ - that prefix marks session variables.
    DECLARE v_balance      DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- A second local, declared with the same type as the column it will hold.
    DECLARE v_credit_limit DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO: read both values from the row in one statement rather than
    --   querying the table twice.
    SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
    INTO   v_balance, v_credit_limit
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- SET: assigns a value to a variable. The calculation is done in the
    --   procedure, not in SQL, and the answer goes into the OUT parameter.
    SET o_available = v_credit_limit - v_balance;
END //

DELIMITER ;

The first call reports 1179.25 for Whiskers & Wags Boutique, whose limit of 6000.00 stands against a balance of 4820.75. The second reports 10000.00 for Companion Care Clinic, which owes nothing against a limit of 10000.00. Two callers, two answers, one copy of the arithmetic.

blocks.text: INOUT: a value that goes in and comes back changed

An `INOUT` parameter is the right choice when the procedure's job is to adjust a number the caller is already holding. A commission run works that way: it starts with a rep's running total and adds the effect of one more sale, at that rep's own rate.

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: demonstrates the third parameter direction.
CREATE PROCEDURE ADD_SALE_TO_COMMISSION(
    IN    i_rep_num     CHAR(2),
    IN    i_sale_amount DECIMAL(9,2),

    -- INOUT: the caller passes a value IN, the procedure changes it, and the new
    --   value goes back OUT through the same parameter. Use it when the answer
    --   depends on what was there before.
    INOUT io_commission DECIMAL(8,2))
BEGIN

    -- A local to hold the rate looked up from the table.
    DECLARE v_rate DECIMAL(4,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO: fetch this rep's commission rate.
    SELECT RATE
    INTO   v_rate
    FROM   REP
    WHERE  REP_NUM = i_rep_num;

    -- SET: the INOUT parameter appears on BOTH sides - its incoming value is
    --   read on the right, and the updated total is written back on the left.
    SET io_commission = io_commission + (i_sale_amount * v_rate);
END //

DELIMITER ;

`@comm` starts at rep 35's stored commission of 39355.00. That rep's rate is 0.07, so a 1200.00 sale adds 84.00 and the procedure hands back 39439.00. Change that `INOUT` to `OUT` and the arithmetic breaks immediately: the incoming 39355.00 would be discarded when the procedure starts, leaving NULL plus 84.00, which is NULL.
Seeing what is stored
Procedures are objects in the database, so the catalog knows about them. In MySQL you can list the ones you have created:

-- SELECT: the catalogue again, this time listing stored routines rather than
--   tables - procedures and functions both appear here.
SELECT ROUTINE_NAME, ROUTINE_TYPE

-- FROM: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES, one row per stored routine on the server.
FROM   INFORMATION_SCHEMA.ROUTINES

-- WHERE: DATABASE() returns the name of the database you are currently connected
--   to, so this narrows the list to your own routines without hard-coding a name.
WHERE  ROUTINE_SCHEMA = DATABASE()
ORDER  BY ROUTINE_NAME;

That query is another place the two engines part company. MySQL keeps this metadata in `INFORMATION_SCHEMA`. SQLite has no `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` at all, and its catalog, `sqlite_master`, lists tables, indexes, views, and triggers because those are the only object types it has. There is no row there for a procedure, because SQLite cannot store one.
To see the text of one procedure rather than a list of names, ask for its definition:

-- SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE: prints the full text of a procedure as the server
--   stored it. This is how you read code somebody else wrote, or recover your
--   own when the script that created it has been lost.
SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE DISP_REP_NAME;

items: I can say in one sentence what a stored procedure is and where it lives.
I know why DELIMITER is needed and that the server never sees it.
I can choose between IN, OUT, and INOUT for a given parameter and defend the choice.
I never give a parameter the same name as a column.
I can write SELECT ... INTO for a lookup on a primary key and read the answer back through a session variable.

blocks.text: A procedure that fails loudly costs you ten minutes. A procedure that fails silently costs you a month, because nobody knows it failed. Error handling is what turns the second kind into the first.

The trouble starts with `SELECT ... INTO`, which expects exactly one row. When it finds none, MySQL does not raise an error. It raises warning 1329, No data - zero rows fetched, selected, or processed, and the procedure carries on to the next statement as though nothing had happened. Warnings are easy to miss, and most application code never looks at them.
Here is a lookup with no handler at all. It is correct for every customer that exists, which is exactly why the flaw survives testing:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: written the obvious way, with no error handling at all -
--   which is exactly what makes it unsafe.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_balance      DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO: fine when the customer exists. When it does not, the
    --   SELECT finds no row, MySQL raises a NOT FOUND warning rather than an
    --   error, and o_balance is left holding whatever it held before. The caller
    --   is never told that anything went wrong.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;

The first `SELECT @bal` reports 3512.50, the balance for Access Pet Center. There is no customer 9999, so the second call assigns nothing, `SHOW WARNINGS` displays warning 1329, and `@bal` comes back NULL, because an `OUT` parameter was set to NULL when the procedure started. Nothing stopped, nothing was recorded, and the only clue is a warning the caller had to ask for.

NULL is at least visibly wrong. The dangerous version returns a number that looks perfectly reasonable. An `INOUT` parameter is not blanked: it arrives holding whatever the caller put in it, and if the lookup assigns nothing, that incoming value is what travels straight back out. A local variable behaves the same way within a single execution: `DECLARE` gives it NULL at the start of every call, but once you have assigned to it, a later failed lookup leaves the earlier value sitting there untouched.

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS STALE_DEMO //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the same trap, made even easier to fall into by using INOUT.
CREATE PROCEDURE STALE_DEMO(
    IN    i_customer_num CHAR(4),

    -- INOUT means the parameter arrives holding the caller's old value, so a
    --   failed lookup leaves that stale value sitting in place.
    INOUT io_balance     DECIMAL(9,2))
BEGIN

    -- No handler, so a miss changes nothing and says nothing.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   io_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Both `SELECT` statements report 3512.50. The second one is a lie: `@bal` still held Access Pet Center's balance from the first call, the `INOUT` parameter carried it into the body, nothing overwrote it, and it came back out as the answer for a customer that does not exist. A credit check built on that answer approves an order for nobody.

blocks.label: The rule worth memorizing
blocks.text: A wrong answer that looks right is worse than an error message. An error stops the work and names the problem. A stale value travels quietly into an invoice, a report, and a decision.
DECLARE ... HANDLER

A handler is a standing instruction: when this condition occurs anywhere in the block, run this statement. You declare it once, at the top of the block, and MySQL applies it for the rest of the block. The shape is `DECLARE`, then an action, then `HANDLER FOR`, then a condition, then one statement, or a `BEGIN ... END` group of statements.

The action is `CONTINUE` or `EXIT`. `CONTINUE` runs the handler statement and then resumes with the statement after the one that raised the condition. `EXIT` runs the handler statement and then leaves the enclosing `BEGIN ... END` block, which for a top-level block means the procedure returns.
Now the same balance lookup, written so that a missing customer is reported instead of hidden:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_CUST_BALANCE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: the safe version of the lookup.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUST_BALANCE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_balance      DECIMAL(9,2),

    -- A second OUT parameter carrying a plain-language status, so the caller
    --   learns what happened as well as what was found.
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE ... HANDLER: registers what to do when a condition arises. CONTINUE
    --   means "run this, then carry on with the next statement"; NOT FOUND is the
    --   condition raised when a SELECT ... INTO matches no row.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND

        -- CONCAT builds a message that names the customer that was missing.
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num);

    -- Set the OUT parameters to known values BEFORE the lookup, so nothing stale
    --   can survive. This line is what kills the previous example's bug.
    SET o_balance = NULL;

    -- The optimistic default, overwritten by the handler if the lookup misses.
    SET o_status  = 'OK';

    -- The lookup itself. If it finds nothing, the handler fires and o_status
    --   changes; if it succeeds, o_status stays 'OK'.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
END //

DELIMITER ;

The first call reports 3512.50 with status OK. The second reports NULL with status No customer numbered 9999. The caller now has something it can test. Notice the two `SET` statements before the query: establishing a known starting state is what makes the outcome unambiguous, whichever path the body takes.

blocks.text: Which conditions you can handle

blocks.caption: Handler conditions in MySQL
rows: A SELECT ... INTO matched no rows. The same condition also covers a cursor fetched past its last row, though no cursors appear in these three sections.
The statement completed but raised a warning, such as a value truncated on its way into a column
Every SQLSTATE class other than 00, 01, and 02
A genuine error: a constraint violation, a duplicate key, or more than one row for a SELECT ... INTO
A single MySQL error number, written FOR 1451, or a SQLSTATE value, written FOR SQLSTATE '23000'

You want that failure handled differently from everything else. An error number names exactly one error; a SQLSTATE value names a family, so '23000' catches a duplicate key as well as a foreign key violation.

blocks.text: The three general conditions cover different SQLSTATE classes and do not overlap, so one procedure can safely declare a `NOT FOUND` handler and a `SQLEXCEPTION` handler at the same time. A missing row goes to the first, a constraint violation to the second. Class 00 means success and needs no handler.
CONTINUE or EXIT

cards.title: CONTINUE
cards.body: Note the problem and keep going. Right when the rest of the body is still safe to run: recording that a lookup came up empty, then finishing a report. Wrong when the statements that follow depend on the value that never arrived, because they will run anyway, on nothing.

cards.title: EXIT
cards.body: Note the problem and stop. Right when the failed statement was a precondition for everything after it: if the customer does not exist, do not update, do not delete, do not log a payment. This is the safer default for any procedure that changes data.

blocks.text: SQLEXCEPTION: catching a real error

`SELECT ... INTO` is equally unhappy with too many rows, but that case is an error rather than a warning: ERROR 1172 (42000), Result consisted of more than one row. With no handler, the procedure stops there and the error surfaces to whoever called it. With a handler, you decide what the caller sees.
This procedure looks a balance up by city, a design that only works while each city holds one customer. KimTay has two in Maple Grove, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: this one looks up on a NON-key column, which is where the
--   other failure mode lives - too many rows rather than none.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_BALANCE_BY_CITY(
    IN  i_city    VARCHAR(20),
    OUT o_balance DECIMAL(9,2),
    OUT o_status  VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE EXIT HANDLER: EXIT means "run this, then STOP the procedure" -
    --   unlike CONTINUE, nothing after the failing statement runs. SQLEXCEPTION
    --   catches any error, including a SELECT ... INTO that matched several rows.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
        SET o_status = CONCAT('Lookup failed for ', i_city, ' - check the city');

    -- Known starting values again.
    SET o_balance = NULL;
    SET o_status  = 'OK';

    -- One city holds one customer and works; another holds two, the INTO cannot
    --   choose between them, and the EXIT handler takes over.
    SELECT BALANCE
    INTO   o_balance
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CITY = i_city;
END //

DELIMITER ;

Northfield holds one customer, Downtown Aquarium & Pets, so the first call reports 1200.00 with status OK. Maple Grove holds two, so the second raises error 1172, the handler catches it, and the caller sees NULL with status Lookup failed for Maple Grove - check the city. The session stays alive and the client sees no error at all. That is the point of catching it, and also the responsibility that comes with catching it: if you swallow an error, you have to report it some other way, or you have rebuilt the silent failure you set out to remove.

blocks.label: Declaration order is fixed
blocks.text: Inside a `BEGIN ... END` block MySQL requires a strict order: `DECLARE` for variables and conditions first, then any cursor declarations, then handler declarations, and only then executable statements. Nothing in these sections uses a cursor, but the slot exists between the two kinds of declaration. Putting a `DECLARE` after a `SET` is a syntax error, and the message points at the `DECLARE` rather than explaining the rule.

blocks.label: Give every procedure a status parameter
blocks.text: An `OUT o_status` costs one line and turns a procedure into something a caller can check. Set it to a known value at the top of the body, overwrite it in each handler, and overwrite it once more when the work finishes successfully. The caller then never has to guess whether anything happened.

items: I can explain why SELECT ... INTO finding no rows is a warning rather than an error.

I know that an OUT parameter starts as NULL, that an INOUT parameter arrives holding the caller's value, and that a local variable starts NULL on every call but keeps whatever it was last assigned during that call.
I can write a NOT FOUND handler and a SQLEXCEPTION handler and say which one fires when.
I can choose CONTINUE or EXIT for a given procedure and defend the choice.
I set a status value at the top of the body so the caller always learns what happened.

blocks.text: Everything so far has read data. Procedures that change data are where the case for putting SQL in the database stops being about convenience and starts being about safety. The reason is short: the procedure carries the `WHERE` clause. It is written once, by someone who knew what they were doing, and it cannot be forgotten at four in the afternoon.
8-6a Changing data with a procedure
Consider the everyday task of adding a charge to a customer's balance. Typed by hand it is one statement. Typed by hand with the last line missing it is a very different statement:

-- The accident. Read it, do not run it: every worked example below
-- assumes the shipped balances are still intact.
-- UPDATE: the table.
UPDATE CUSTOMER

-- SET with no WHERE: every customer's balance goes up by 250. The statement is
--   perfectly valid SQL, which is precisely the danger - wrapping this logic in
--   a procedure that always carries its own WHERE clause is how you stop a
--   missing line from reaching production.
SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + 250.00;

That succeeds. MySQL reports Query OK, 4 rows affected, and every KimTay customer has been charged: Access Pet Center rises to 3762.50, Downtown Aquarium & Pets to 1450.00, Companion Care Clinic to 250.00 for an order it never placed, and Whiskers & Wags Boutique to 5070.75. There is no syntax error to catch it, and outside a transaction there is nothing to roll back.
Now the same operation as a procedure. The `WHERE` clause is part of the stored definition and the customer number is a required parameter, so there is no version of this that runs without a target:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS UPD_CUST_BALANCE //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: an UPDATE wrapped safely, so the WHERE clause can never be
--   forgotten and a missing customer is reported rather than ignored.
CREATE PROCEDURE UPD_CUST_BALANCE(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    IN  i_amount       DECIMAL(9,2),
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN

    -- A local to hold the customer's name, used in the status message.
    DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35);

    -- EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND: if the customer does not exist, stop before the
    --   UPDATE ever runs and say so. EXIT rather than CONTINUE is deliberate.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num, ' - nothing changed');

    -- The lookup does double duty: it fetches the name AND proves the customer
    --   exists. A miss here fires the handler and the procedure ends.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME
    INTO   v_name
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- The change itself, reached only when the customer is known to exist.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + i_amount

    -- The WHERE clause is written into the procedure once and cannot be left off
    --   by a caller in a hurry.
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- Report exactly what was done, naming the customer and the amount.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Balance for ', v_name, ' changed by ', i_amount);
END //

DELIMITER ;

The lookup at the top is doing real work. It fetches the name for the status message, but more importantly it is an existence test. If the customer is not there, `NOT FOUND` fires, and because the handler is an `EXIT` handler the `UPDATE` never runs at all.

The first call reports Balance for Access Pet Center changed by 250.00, and the listing that follows shows 1120 at 3762.50 while 1225, 1310, and 1420 sit untouched at 1200.00, 0.00, and 4820.75. The second call reports No customer numbered 9999 - nothing changed, and no row anywhere moved. This example does change the shipped data; the cleanup at the end of the section puts 1120 back.
