blocks.text: An update procedure with a transaction

When a procedure changes data, a handler is the natural place to undo partial work. This one reduces stock as an item ships, wraps the change in a transaction, and rolls back if anything goes wrong. Notice the declaration order: the local variable first, then the handlers, then the executable statements.

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS SHIP_ITEM //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: a procedure that changes data inside a transaction, with two
--   different handlers for two different kinds of failure.
CREATE PROCEDURE SHIP_ITEM(
    IN  i_item_id     CHAR(4),
    IN  i_qty_shipped SMALLINT,
    OUT o_status      VARCHAR(60))
BEGIN
    DECLARE v_description VARCHAR(30);

    -- EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION with a BEGIN ... END block: a handler can run
    --   several statements, not just one, when it is wrapped like this.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
    BEGIN

        -- ROLLBACK first: undo any half-finished change before reporting.
        ROLLBACK;
        SET o_status = 'Shipment failed - stock left unchanged';
    END;

    -- A second handler for a different condition. NOT FOUND is not an error, so
    --   it needs its own handler; SQLEXCEPTION would never catch it.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No item numbered ', i_item_id);

    -- Look up the item, which also proves it exists before anything is changed.
    SELECT DESCRIPTION
    INTO   v_description
    FROM   ITEM
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = i_item_id;

    -- START TRANSACTION: open the safety net around the change.
    START TRANSACTION;

    -- The change itself.
    UPDATE ITEM
    SET    ON_HAND = ON_HAND - i_qty_shipped
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = i_item_id;

    -- COMMIT: reached only if the UPDATE raised nothing. If it had, the
    --   SQLEXCEPTION handler would have rolled back and ended the procedure
    --   before this line.
    COMMIT;

    -- The success message, built from the description looked up earlier.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Shipped ', i_qty_shipped, ' of ', v_description);
END //

DELIMITER ;

The first call reports Shipped 3 of Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb and leaves `ON_HAND` at 45, down from 48. The second reports No item numbered ZZ99 and never opens a transaction, because the `EXIT` handler for `NOT FOUND` returns before `START TRANSACTION` is reached.

The `SQLEXCEPTION` handler is the insurance policy, and it is worth being exact about when it earns its keep. KimTay's `ON_HAND` is a plain `SMALLINT`, so shipping more units than exist would quietly produce a negative number rather than an error, which is a data-quality problem this procedure does not solve. Declare the column `SMALLINT UNSIGNED` instead and the same subtraction raises ERROR 1264, out of range value, under MySQL's default strict SQL mode. Then the handler does its job: the `ROLLBACK` undoes the change and the caller is told the shipment failed.
8-6b Deleting data with a procedure

Everything true of `UPDATE` is more true of `DELETE`. An `UPDATE` that hits every row can sometimes be reasoned back out of, because the old values are often recoverable from somewhere. A `DELETE` that hits every row leaves nothing to reason with.

-- The accident. Read it, do not run it.
-- DELETE with no WHERE: every customer row is removed in one statement. Nothing
--   warns you, and outside a transaction nothing brings them back. This is the
--   statement the procedure below exists to make impossible.
DELETE FROM CUSTOMER;

Against the KimTay data this one fails, with ERROR 1451 (23000), Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails, because invoices 50710, 50711, and 50712 point at customers 1120, 1420, and 1225. The whole statement is rolled back and no rows are removed. That is a foreign key doing its job, and it is not a rescue to count on: on any table with no children, the same statement empties it without complaint.
The procedure version takes the customer number as a parameter, confirms that the customer exists, and turns the foreign key error into a sentence a person can read:

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS DEL_CUSTOMER //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: a delete that can only ever remove one named row, and that
--   explains itself whichever way it ends.
CREATE PROCEDURE DEL_CUSTOMER(
    IN  i_customer_num CHAR(4),
    OUT o_status       VARCHAR(70))
BEGIN
    DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35);

    -- Handler 1 - an actual error. The likeliest one here is a foreign key
    --   violation: the customer still has invoices pointing at it.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
        SET o_status = CONCAT('Could not delete ', i_customer_num, ' - invoices still reference it');

    -- Handler 2 - not an error at all, just nothing found. Two conditions, two
    --   handlers, two different messages.
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
        SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num);

    -- Fetch the name, and in doing so confirm the customer exists.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME
    INTO   v_name
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- The delete, with its WHERE clause built in permanently.
    DELETE FROM CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;

    -- Reached only when the delete succeeded.
    SET o_status = CONCAT('Deleted ', v_name);
END //

DELIMITER ;
Two handlers, two different failures. `NOT FOUND` belongs to SQLSTATE class 02 and `SQLEXCEPTION` covers the classes outside 00, 01, and 02, so they cannot both claim the same condition.

Three calls, three endings. Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so 1310 is removed and the status reads Deleted Companion Care Clinic. Access Pet Center appears on invoice 50710, so the `DELETE` raises the foreign key error, the `SQLEXCEPTION` handler catches it, and the status reads Could not delete 1120 - invoices still reference it, with the row still in place. Customer 9999 never existed, so `NOT FOUND` fires before the `DELETE` is reached. The final listing shows 1120, 1225, and 1420 remaining.
Put Companion Care Clinic back before you move on, so that the rest of the course's examples still match:

-- INSERT INTO with no column list: put the deleted customer back, supplying a
--   value for all nine columns in the table's own order. This is the tidy-up
--   step, so the rest of the module works against the shipped data.
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER
VALUES ('1310', 'Companion Care Clinic', '89 River Rd.', 'Maple Grove', 'OH',
        '44601', 0.00, 10000.00, '20');
The safety argument, stated plainly

cards.title: Typed by hand
cards.body: The WHERE clause is rewritten every time, by whoever is at the keyboard. A missing line, a stray semicolon, or the wrong window changes every row in the table. Existence is never checked, failures arrive as raw error codes, and the only record of what was intended is in somebody's memory.

cards.title: Run as a procedure
cards.body: The WHERE clause is stored once and cannot be dropped. The key is a required parameter, so nothing runs without a target. Existence is verified before the change, failures come back as sentences through a status parameter, and the definition can be reviewed and version controlled like any other code.

blocks.text: There is a second, sharper version of the argument that has nothing to do with typing. Privileges in MySQL can be granted on a procedure rather than on a table. Give an account the right to execute `DEL_CUSTOMER` and withhold `DELETE` on `CUSTOMER`, and that account can retire a closed account through the checked, single-row path and has no way to issue a bare `DELETE` at all.

blocks.label: Why that actually works: SQL SECURITY DEFINER
blocks.text: The arrangement depends on a default worth saying out loud. Unless you write otherwise, MySQL creates a procedure with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER`, so the body runs with the privileges of the account that defined it, not the account that called it. That is why the clerk needs `EXECUTE` and nothing more: the `DELETE` inside the procedure is performed on the definer's authority. Create the same procedure with `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` and the clerk would need `DELETE` on `CUSTOMER` after all, which is precisely the privilege you were trying to withhold.

blocks.label: Engine note
blocks.text: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, and `CREATE USER` are MySQL and Oracle. SQLite has no user accounts and no privilege system whatsoever, so none of these statements exist there - permission in SQLite is whatever the operating system says about the database file. Replace `KIMTAY` with the name of your own schema before running them, and use a real password rather than the placeholder.
Cleaning up

Two of the examples in this section changed real rows: `UPD_CUST_BALANCE` added 250.00 to customer 1120, and `SHIP_ITEM` took 3 units off item CF21. Put both back to their shipped values, so that every later example in the course still matches. Writing the restore as an assignment rather than an adjustment makes it safe to run twice:
Procedures persist until you drop them. When you have finished working through these three sections, remove the ones you created:

items: I can write an update procedure whose WHERE clause uses a required parameter.
I use an EXIT handler so that a missing row prevents the change instead of quietly matching nothing.
I can wrap a change in a transaction and ROLLBACK from inside a SQLEXCEPTION handler.
I can explain why a foreign key error is a better outcome than a successful delete.
I can state the privilege argument, EXECUTE on the procedure rather than DELETE on the table, and I know it works because MySQL defaults a procedure to SQL SECURITY DEFINER.
I restore any row an example changed before moving on.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: procedures, parameters, and CALL

questions.scenarioTitle: Access Pet Center's credit check
questions.stem: KimTay wants one place that reports how much credit a customer has left. The procedure declares IN i_customer_num CHAR(4) and OUT o_available DECIMAL(9,2). What does the OUT mode actually change about the call?
options: The caller must supply a starting value for o_available or MySQL refuses to run the procedure
The procedure hands a value back through the session variable named in that position of the CALL
The procedure prints the value to the screen on its own, with no SELECT needed afterward
The computed value is written into a new column of CUSTOMER when the procedure finishes
optionNotes: Backwards. An OUT parameter is set to NULL as the procedure starts, so anything the caller passed is discarded; INOUT is the mode that carries a starting value in.
Correct. OUT means the value travels from the procedure to the caller, which is why the argument has to be a writable session variable such as @avail rather than a literal.
A CALL displays nothing on its own. Only a bare SELECT inside the body returns a result set; an OUT parameter has to be selected afterward to be seen.
Confuses returning a value with storing one. Nothing in this procedure changes the database; CREDIT_LIMIT minus BALANCE is computed fresh on every call.
questions.takeaway: OUT is a one-way channel out of the procedure, and the caller reads it by selecting the session variable it named in the CALL.

questions.scenarioTitle: A rep lookup that matches everybody
questions.stem: A developer names a parameter REP_NUM, the same as the column, and writes WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM in the body. Calling it with '35' fails with ERROR 1172, result consisted of more than one row. What happened?
options: MySQL reads both sides of the comparison as the parameter, so the test is always true and all three reps match
MySQL reads both sides as the column, and a column compared with itself never matches any row
CHAR(2) values cannot be compared with a parameter of the same type unless you write an explicit CAST
SELECT ... INTO is not permitted inside a procedure body and has to be replaced by a cursor
optionNotes: Correct. When a name could mean a parameter or a column, MySQL resolves it as the parameter, so the condition reduces to a value equal to itself and every row in REP qualifies.
The resolution goes the other way, and a column compared with itself would match every row rather than none, since every REP_NUM in the shipped data holds a value.
No cast is involved. Comparing two CHAR(2) values is ordinary, and a type problem would not produce a row-count error.
SELECT ... INTO is the normal way to fetch one row inside a procedure. A cursor is for stepping through many rows, which is a different problem.
questions.takeaway: Prefix parameter names so they can never collide with column names, because the error MySQL reports describes a symptom rather than the cause.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's first procedure in Workbench
questions.stem: A student pastes a CREATE PROCEDURE whose body holds three statements into the mysql client and gets a syntax error at the first semicolon inside the body. What fixes it?
options: Remove the semicolons inside the body so that the procedure contains one long statement
Wrap the body in START TRANSACTION and COMMIT so the client treats it as a single unit
Change the client's terminator with DELIMITER //, end the procedure with //, then restore it with DELIMITER ;
Create the procedure from a different schema, because a procedure cannot be stored in the schema it reads
optionNotes: The body needs those semicolons; every statement between BEGIN and END must be terminated. Removing them produces a different syntax error.
A transaction groups changes to data. It says nothing about where the client believes one statement ends and the next begins.
Correct. The client, not the server, is splitting the text at the first semicolon, so changing the terminator makes it send the whole CREATE PROCEDURE as one statement.
A procedure normally lives in the same schema as the tables it uses, and its location has nothing to do with a statement terminator.
questions.takeaway: DELIMITER is a client instruction that keeps a semicolon-filled procedure body from being chopped into fragments before it reaches the server.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: handlers and silent failure

questions.scenarioTitle: A balance lookup for a customer who is not there
questions.stem: GET_CUST_BALANCE_UNSAFE has no handler at all. It runs SELECT BALANCE INTO o_balance for customer 9999, which does not exist in KimTay's data. What does the caller get?
options: An error that halts the procedure, since SELECT ... INTO requires exactly one row to work
The balance of whichever customer the procedure looked up last, quietly reused
NULL in the OUT parameter, plus warning 1329, which the caller has to ask for to see
Zero in the OUT parameter, because MySQL treats a customer with no row as owing nothing
optionNotes: Zero rows raises a warning, not an error. Too many rows is the error case; too few passes by quietly and the body keeps running.

That is the hazard with an INOUT parameter, which arrives holding whatever the caller passed, or with a local variable already assigned earlier in the same execution. This OUT parameter was set to NULL when the procedure started.
Correct. Nothing is assigned, the OUT parameter keeps the NULL it started with, and MySQL raises warning 1329 that no data was fetched.
MySQL never invents a value. A missing row and a balance of 0.00, which is what Companion Care Clinic actually has, are different facts.
questions.takeaway: Without a handler, a lookup that finds nothing reports nothing, and the only trace is a warning almost no caller checks.

questions.scenarioTitle: Two customers in Maple Grove
questions.stem: A procedure runs SELECT BALANCE INTO o_balance FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CITY = i_city and is called with 'Maple Grove', which matches both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. Which handler catches that?
options: A CONTINUE handler for NOT FOUND, since finding two rows means no single row was found
An EXIT handler for SQLWARNING, since MySQL only warns when extra rows are available
No handler is needed, because MySQL keeps the first row it reads and discards the other
An EXIT handler for SQLEXCEPTION, because error 1172 is a genuine error rather than a warning
optionNotes: NOT FOUND covers SQLSTATE class 02, which means zero rows. Two rows is the opposite problem and belongs to a different class entirely.
SQLWARNING covers class 01. Too many rows for SELECT ... INTO is error 1172, SQLSTATE 42000, which is not a warning and would slip past this handler.
MySQL refuses rather than picking one, which is the safe choice; silently keeping an arbitrary row would produce a plausible wrong answer.
Correct. SQLEXCEPTION covers every SQLSTATE class other than 00, 01, and 02, which includes the more-than-one-row error.
questions.takeaway: NOT FOUND, SQLWARNING, and SQLEXCEPTION cover different SQLSTATE classes, so one procedure can declare several handlers without them overlapping.

questions.scenarioTitle: A delete routine that keeps going after it fails
questions.stem: A procedure that removes a customer declares a CONTINUE handler for SQLEXCEPTION that sets a status message, and three more statements follow the DELETE. What is the risk of choosing CONTINUE here?
options: The three statements after the failed DELETE still run, so the procedure finishes half-done work
A CONTINUE handler is not allowed to assign to an OUT parameter, so the status never reaches the caller
CONTINUE rolls the whole procedure back automatically, discarding the status message along with it
CONTINUE retries the failed statement over and over until it succeeds or the connection times out
optionNotes: Correct. CONTINUE resumes at the statement after the one that failed, so anything written on the assumption that the DELETE worked runs anyway, against unchanged data.
Handlers assign to OUT parameters routinely; that is how a status message reaches the caller in every example in this section.
No handler rolls a transaction back on its own. A ROLLBACK happens only if you write one, which is why the SHIP_ITEM handler includes it explicitly.
Neither CONTINUE nor EXIT retries anything. CONTINUE moves forward and EXIT leaves the block; MySQL has no retry action.
questions.takeaway: Use EXIT when the statements that follow depend on the one that failed, and save CONTINUE for cases where the rest of the body is still safe to run.

quizzes.heading: Check yourself: update and delete procedures

questions.scenarioTitle: A charge posted to Access Pet Center
questions.stem: Against the shipped data, a clerk runs CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('1120', 250.00, @status). What is Access Pet Center's balance afterward, and what makes this safer than typing the UPDATE by hand?
options: 3262.50, and it is safer because a procedure always subtracts rather than adds the amount passed in
3762.50, and it is safer because the WHERE clause is stored once and cannot be left off
3762.50, and it is safer because MySQL will not allow a procedure to change more than one row
250.00, and it is safer because the procedure replaces the old balance with the value supplied
optionNotes: The body adds: BALANCE = BALANCE + i_amount. Pass a negative amount to reduce a balance; the direction is the caller's choice, not the procedure's.
Correct. 3512.50 plus 250.00 is 3762.50, and the stored WHERE clause on the required parameter is what keeps the change to one customer.
The arithmetic is right but the reason is wrong. A procedure may change every row in a table; being stored places no limit on the row count.
That would be an assignment rather than an adjustment. This procedure adds to the existing balance, so 3512.50 is the starting point, not something discarded.
questions.takeaway: The safety comes from the WHERE clause living in the stored definition beside a required key parameter, not from anything MySQL enforces on its own.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring Companion Care Clinic
questions.stem: DEL_CUSTOMER is called for 1310, then for 1120. Companion Care Clinic has no invoice; Access Pet Center appears on invoice 50710. What do the two calls report?
options: Both succeed, because a stored procedure runs with elevated rights that bypass foreign keys
Both fail, because a DELETE issued inside a procedure needs an explicit COMMIT to take effect
1310 is deleted; 1120 raises a foreign key error that the SQLEXCEPTION handler turns into a message
1310 raises NOT FOUND because it has no invoice, and 1120 is deleted along with its invoice lines

questions.scenarioTitle: Locking down KimTay's billing clerk
questions.stem: KimTay wants a clerk to be able to remove a closed customer account through the checked path, but never to be able to issue a bare DELETE against CUSTOMER. Which arrangement delivers that?
options: Grant DELETE on CUSTOMER and trust the clerk to always include a WHERE clause
Grant SELECT on CUSTOMER only, since a stored procedure needs no privileges of its own
Ask the clerk to run every delete inside a transaction so a mistake can be rolled back later
Grant EXECUTE on DEL_CUSTOMER and withhold DELETE on the CUSTOMER table entirely
optionNotes: This is exactly the exposure to remove. Once DELETE on the table is granted, one forgotten line empties it, and no amount of care makes that impossible.
SELECT alone cannot delete anything, so the clerk could not do the job at all; the account still has to be permitted to run the procedure.
A transaction helps only if the mistake is noticed before the COMMIT, and it does nothing to stop a bare DELETE from being issued in the first place.

Correct. The privilege is attached to the procedure, and because MySQL creates procedures with SQL SECURITY DEFINER by default, the DELETE inside runs on the definer's authority, so the only delete available to that account is the one that takes a customer number and checks it first.
questions.takeaway: Granting EXECUTE on a procedure instead of DELETE on a table turns a policy about how deletes should be done into a rule the server enforces, provided the procedure keeps the default SQL SECURITY DEFINER.

matchers.heading: Anatomy of a stored procedure
matchers.prompt: Each card is one line taken from the KimTay procedures in 8-4 through 8-6. Drop each line into the part of the procedure it belongs to. Every card fits exactly one zone.

zones.label: Work statement
zones.hint: Reads or changes the stored data

cards.text: IN i_customer_num CHAR(4)
cards.why: It carries the customer number from the caller into the procedure and cannot send anything back.

cards.text: OUT o_status VARCHAR(60)
cards.why: It carries a message back out to the session variable named in that position of the CALL.

cards.text: DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(35);
cards.why: It creates scratch storage that exists only between BEGIN and END and is invisible to the caller.

cards.text: DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET o_status = CONCAT('No customer numbered ', i_customer_num);
cards.why: It arms a reaction to SQLSTATE class 02 and then resumes with the statement after the failure.

cards.text: DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION SET o_status = CONCAT('Could not delete ', i_customer_num, ' - invoices still reference it');
cards.why: It arms a reaction to a genuine error and leaves the block rather than carrying on.

cards.text: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME INTO v_name FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
cards.why: It reads the CUSTOMER table, which is work on stored data, and doubles as an existence test.

cards.text: UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = BALANCE + i_amount WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
cards.why: It changes stored data, and its WHERE clause is the thing the procedure exists to protect.

cards.text: CALL UPD_CUST_BALANCE('1120', 250.00, @status);
cards.why: It is typed by whoever runs the procedure, outside the definition, and supplies the arguments.

sections.title: Selecting Multiple Rows with a Procedure

blocks.text: Every procedure you have written so far has worked on one row. You passed in a customer number, the procedure ran a `SELECT ... INTO`, and one set of values landed in the variables. That works because the query could only ever match one row: `CUSTOMER_NUM` is the primary key.

Real requests are rarely that tidy. "Review every customer in rep 20's territory" matches two rows in the KimTay data, Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. "Log every line on invoice 50710" matches two rows. A procedure that has to look at each of those rows in turn needs a different tool, and that tool is a cursor.

blocks.label: Engine note, said once
blocks.text: Cursors, handlers, and loops are MySQL stored-program features. None of the procedure code in this section runs in this page's sandbox, because the sandbox is SQLite and SQLite has no CREATE PROCEDURE, no DECLARE, and no cursors. Read the procedure code in the code blocks and run it in MySQL Workbench. What the sandboxes in this section do run is ordinary SQL: the queries the cursors are built on, and at the end the set-based statements that replace one of the loops entirely.
8-7a Using a Cursor
Start from what already works. Inside a procedure, this statement copies one row into two variables:

-- SELECT ... INTO: the one-row form you have already used. It works only when
--   the query returns exactly one row, which is why it is safe on a primary key
--   lookup and dangerous on anything else.
SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT

    -- INTO: two columns land in two variables, matched by position.
    INTO v_balance, v_credit_limit
    FROM CUSTOMER

    -- Filtering on the key is what guarantees the single row.
    WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = i_customer_num;
Now change the condition from a primary key to a rep number. The query is still legal SQL, but it no longer returns one row:

blocks.starter:
-- Rep 20's territory: the CUSTOMER rows whose REP_NUM is '20'.
-- Run this and count the rows. That count is why a cursor exists.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- The four columns a stored procedure would read INTO its local variables.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
-- The procedure's parameter goes here in place of the literal.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
-- ORDER BY matters more than usual for a cursor: it fixes the order the rows
-- will be handed over, one at a time.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Two rows come back: 1120 Access Pet Center and 1310 Companion Care Clinic. Ask yourself which one a single set of variables could hold.

blocks.text: Two rows come back. Put that same query behind `SELECT ... INTO` in a MySQL procedure and the procedure stops with `ERROR 1172: Result consisted of more than one row`. There is no partial credit and no silent first row. `SELECT ... INTO` demands exactly one row.

blocks.label: Cursor
blocks.text: A cursor is a named pointer into the result set of a SELECT. Instead of assigning a whole result to variables at once, a cursor holds the rows and hands them to you one at a time, in order, on demand. Think of it as a bookmark that starts above the first row and moves down one row every time you ask for the next one.
You declare a cursor by giving it a name and the query it stands for. Declaring does not run the query. It records the definition so the procedure can open it later:

-- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor is a query held ready, so the procedure can
--   walk its rows ONE AT A TIME. This line only defines it - nothing runs yet,
--   and the SELECT below is not executed until OPEN.
DECLARE cust_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- The query the cursor will walk. Four columns, so four variables will be
    --   needed to receive each row.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
    FROM CUSTOMER

    -- A cursor query may use a parameter exactly like any other query.
    WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num

    -- ORDER BY matters more than usual here: it fixes the order the rows will be
    --   handed to you in, one by one.
    ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

Two details in that declaration earn their keep. The query refers to `i_rep_num`, the procedure's own parameter, so one cursor definition serves every rep. And it carries `ORDER BY`. A loop reads rows in the order the cursor produces them, so if the order matters to your logic or to a report, say so in the cursor query.

blocks.label: Declaration order is a rule, not a style
blocks.text: MySQL requires every DECLARE to sit at the top of the BEGIN block in a fixed order: variables and conditions first, then cursor declarations, then handler declarations. Put the handler above the cursor and the procedure will not compile. Name variables so they cannot collide with column names, which is why these examples use the `v_` prefix for local variables and `i_` for IN parameters.
8-7b Opening a Cursor
Declaring a cursor is paperwork. Opening it is the moment the work happens:

items: MySQL runs the cursor's SELECT, using whatever values the parameters and variables hold right now.
The result set is built and held for this cursor.
The cursor position is set just above the first row, not on it. Nothing has been copied into your variables yet.
If the query matches no rows at all, `OPEN` still succeeds. You find out that the result is empty on the first FETCH, not here.

blocks.label: Open once, then close
blocks.text: Opening a cursor that is already open raises `ERROR 1325: Cursor is already open`, and fetching from a cursor that was never opened raises `ERROR 1326: Cursor is not open`. One OPEN, one loop, one CLOSE. If a procedure needs to walk the same rows twice, close the cursor and open it again.
8-7c Fetching Rows from a Cursor
`FETCH` moves the cursor down one row and copies that row's column values into variables:

-- FETCH ... INTO: moves the cursor on by one row and copies that row's values
--   into the listed variables. The variables must match the cursor's SELECT list
--   in number, order and type. One FETCH gets exactly one row, which is why a
--   loop is needed to reach them all.
FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                       v_balance, v_credit_limit;

The match is positional. The variable list must have exactly as many variables as the cursor query has columns, in the same order, with compatible types. The cursor above selects four columns, so the FETCH names four variables. Get the count wrong and MySQL reports `ERROR 1328: Incorrect number of FETCH variables`. Get the order wrong and the procedure runs happily while writing a balance into a name.

One FETCH gives you one row. To reach them all, the FETCH goes inside a loop, and the loop needs a way to know it has run out of rows. That is what the NOT FOUND handler does. When a FETCH is attempted past the last row, MySQL raises the NOT FOUND condition; the handler catches it and sets a flag you control:

-- DECLARE ... DEFAULT: a flag variable, starting at 0 meaning "not finished".
DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

-- CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND: when a FETCH runs past the last row, NOT FOUND
--   is raised. This handler sets the flag and lets execution carry on, which is
--   how the loop learns that the rows have run out.
DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

-- LOOP with a LABEL: cust_loop names the loop so it can be left by name.
cust_loop: LOOP

    -- Read the next row into the variables.
    FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name,
                           v_balance, v_credit_limit;

    -- Test the flag IMMEDIATELY after the fetch. If the fetch failed, the
    --   variables still hold the PREVIOUS row, so processing them here would
    --   duplicate the last row - a classic off-by-one in cursor code.
    IF v_done = 1 THEN

        -- LEAVE: jumps out of the named loop. Without it this runs forever.
        LEAVE cust_loop;
    END IF;

    -- work on the row that was retrieved goes here
-- END LOOP: sends control back to the top for the next row.
END LOOP cust_loop;

Read that loop the way MySQL runs it. `LOOP` repeats forever until something leaves it. The label `cust_loop` gives `LEAVE` a target. `CONTINUE` on the handler means "after handling the condition, carry on with the next statement" rather than abandoning the block, which is what lets the very next `IF` see the flag and exit cleanly.

blocks.label: Test the flag immediately after FETCH
blocks.text: A failed FETCH does not blank out your variables. They still hold the previous row's values. If you do the work first and test `v_done` at the bottom of the loop, the last row gets processed twice: once for real, once from the leftovers of the FETCH that found nothing. The test belongs on the line right after the FETCH, before any use of the fetched values.

Use a `CONTINUE` handler here, not an `EXIT` handler. An `EXIT HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND` ends the enclosing block the moment the rows run out, which skips your CLOSE and any summary work you meant to do after the loop.
8-7d Closing a Cursor
When the loop ends, release the result set:

-- CLOSE: releases the cursor and the resources the server was holding for it.
--   Always close what you open, so a long-running procedure does not accumulate
--   open cursors.
CLOSE cust_cursor;

items: The memory holding the rows is freed and the cursor name becomes available to OPEN again.
MySQL closes a cursor automatically at the end of the block that declared it, but write the CLOSE anyway: it documents the lifecycle and it matters in long procedures that open several cursors.
Closing a cursor that is not open raises `ERROR 1326`, so do not put a CLOSE in a path that may run twice.
After CLOSE, the variables keep the values from the last successful FETCH. That is fine to use for a summary line, as long as you know that is where the values came from.

blocks.text: 8-7e Writing a Complete Procedure Using a Cursor

Now assemble the pieces against KimTay. The goal: for one rep, walk that rep's customers, work out how much credit each one has left, mark anyone with less than $5,000 of room for a follow-up call, and record the results so the DBA can read them back.
A MySQL procedure has nowhere to "print" a row, so the procedure writes its findings to a table. Create that table first:

-- DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: clear out any table left behind by an earlier run, so
--   this script can be re-run from the top.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS CUST_REVIEW;

-- CREATE TABLE: somewhere for the procedure to write its results. A stored
--   procedure that loops over rows usually has to put its output somewhere, and
--   a small result table is the simplest place.
CREATE TABLE CUST_REVIEW
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),

     -- The computed figure the procedure will work out per customer.
     AVAILABLE_CREDIT DECIMAL(9,2),

     -- The verdict, chosen by an IF inside the loop.
     REVIEW_NOTE VARCHAR(10));

items.title: Stage 1: the shell
items.body: Parameter, variables, cursor, handler, OPEN and CLOSE. It compiles and runs and does nothing. That is exactly the point: get the declarations legal before adding logic.

items.title: Stage 2: the loop
items.body: Add the labelled LOOP, the FETCH, and the LEAVE test. Now the procedure walks every row and still produces no output, so any error you see is a cursor error, not a logic error.

items.title: Stage 3: the work
items.body: Put the per-row calculation and the INSERT inside the loop. Only now is there anything to get wrong about the business rule.

blocks.text: Stage 1. Note the declaration order: variables, then the cursor, then the handler.
Stage 2. Add the loop between the OPEN and the CLOSE. Only the middle of the procedure changes:
Stage 3. Fill in the loop body and the procedure is finished:
Run it for rep 20 and read the results back:

-- CALL: run the review for one rep. The procedure returns nothing directly -
--   its output is the rows it wrote into CUST_REVIEW.
CALL REP_CREDIT_REVIEW('20');

-- SELECT: read the results table to see what the loop produced, one row per
--   customer the cursor walked.
SELECT * FROM CUST_REVIEW
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

Two rows in, two rows out, each one the product of a separate trip through the loop. Access Pet Center has 7500.00 minus 3512.50, which is 3987.50 of room and lands under the threshold. Companion Care Clinic has spent nothing against a 10000.00 limit and needs no action.

blocks.label: Why DELIMITER wraps all of this
blocks.text: The procedure body is full of semicolons, and the MySQL client would otherwise treat the first one as the end of the CREATE PROCEDURE statement. `DELIMITER //` tells the client to end statements at `//` instead, and `DELIMITER ;` puts it back afterward. It is a client instruction, not SQL, so it never appears inside the procedure.
8-7f Using More Complex Cursors

Nothing about a cursor restricts it to one table. The cursor query is an ordinary SELECT, so joins, calculated columns, GROUP BY, and HAVING are all fair game. Here is a cursor over a four-table join that also computes a line total:

-- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor's query can be as complex as any other. This
--   one joins four tables, and the procedure still walks the result one row at a
--   time exactly as before.
DECLARE line_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- Three stored columns and one calculated column. A cursor column does not
    --   have to correspond to anything stored.
    SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION,
           L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE
    FROM CUSTOMER C

    -- Hop 1 - customer to invoice.
    JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM

    -- Hop 2 - invoice to line item.
    JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

    -- Hop 3 - line item to item.
    JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID

    -- The parameter filters the joined rows.
    WHERE C.REP_NUM = i_rep_num

    -- Fixes the order the rows will be fetched in.
    ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION;

Four tables are needed because the four selected columns live in three of them and INVOICE_LINE ties them together: CUSTOMER_NAME comes from CUSTOMER, INVOICE_NUM from INVOICE, DESCRIPTION from ITEM, and the line total is computed from INVOICE_LINE. The FETCH for this cursor needs four variables, and the fourth one receives a calculated value rather than a stored column, so declare it wide enough for the product: `DECLARE v_line_total DECIMAL(9,2);`.
Run the underlying query to see the rows the loop would walk. The cursor's parameter is written out as a literal, so the statement is plain SQL and runs here:

blocks.text: A cursor query can also read more than one parameter. This procedure takes a rep and a minimum line total, so the same code answers "every line over $50 in rep 65's territory" and "every line over $10 in rep 20's":

-- DROP TABLE IF EXISTS: make the script re-runnable.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS BIG_LINE_LOG;

-- CREATE TABLE: the destination for whatever the procedure finds. Its columns
--   match the four the cursor returns.
CREATE TABLE BIG_LINE_LOG
    (CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),
     INVOICE_NUM CHAR(5),
     DESCRIPTION VARCHAR(30),
     LINE_TOTAL DECIMAL(9,2));

DELIMITER //

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS BIG_LINE_ITEMS //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: two parameters this time, and both are used inside the
--   cursor's query rather than in the loop.
CREATE PROCEDURE BIG_LINE_ITEMS (IN i_rep_num CHAR(2),
                                 IN i_min_total DECIMAL(7,2))
BEGIN

    -- The finished flag.
    DECLARE v_done INT DEFAULT 0;

    -- One variable per cursor column, in the same order.
    DECLARE v_customer_name VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE v_invoice_num CHAR(5);
    DECLARE v_description VARCHAR(30);
    DECLARE v_line_total DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- The cursor over a four-table join.
    DECLARE line_cursor CURSOR FOR
        SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION,
               L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE
        FROM CUSTOMER C
        JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
        JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM
        JOIN ITEM T ON L.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID
        WHERE C.REP_NUM = i_rep_num

        -- The second parameter filters on the CALCULATION, not on a stored
        --   column. Doing the filtering here rather than inside the loop means
        --   fewer rows are ever fetched - the database is better at discarding
        --   rows than your loop is.
          AND L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE >= i_min_total
        ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, T.DESCRIPTION;

    -- The handler that ends the loop.
    DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;

    -- Run the query.
    OPEN line_cursor;

    -- Walk the rows.
    line_loop: LOOP
        FETCH line_cursor INTO v_customer_name, v_invoice_num,
                               v_description, v_line_total;
        IF v_done = 1 THEN
            LEAVE line_loop;
        END IF;

        -- The only work per row: copy it into the log table. Because the cursor
        --   already filtered, no IF is needed here.
        INSERT INTO BIG_LINE_LOG
               (CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE_NUM, DESCRIPTION, LINE_TOTAL)
        VALUES (v_customer_name, v_invoice_num, v_description, v_line_total);
    END LOOP line_loop;

    -- Tidy up.
    CLOSE line_cursor;
END //

DELIMITER ;

-- CALL: rep 65, lines worth 50.00 or more. Change either argument and the same
--   procedure answers a different question.
CALL BIG_LINE_ITEMS('65', 50.00);

blocks.text: A cursor can also walk grouped results. Each FETCH then delivers one group, not one base-table row:

-- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: a cursor over a GROUPED query. Each row the cursor
--   hands back is a summary of several underlying rows, which is fine - the
--   cursor neither knows nor cares how its query was built.
DECLARE invoice_cursor CURSOR FOR

    -- Two grouping columns and one aggregate.
    SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME,
           SUM(L.NUM_ORDERED * L.QUOTED_PRICE)
    FROM INVOICE I

    -- Hop 1 - invoice to customer, for the name.
    JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM

    -- Hop 2 - invoice to its line items, for the money.
    JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

    -- GROUP BY: one row per invoice, so the cursor walks invoices rather than
    --   lines. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list appears here.
    GROUP BY I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME
    ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM;

JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM
JOIN INVOICE_LINE L ON I.INVOICE_NUM = L.INVOICE_NUM

ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM;

blocks.label: Complexity lives in the query, not the loop
blocks.text: Whether the cursor selects from one table, four joined tables, or a GROUP BY, the loop code is identical: OPEN, FETCH into a matching list of variables, test the flag, do the work, CLOSE. Push as much filtering and calculating as you can into the cursor query so the loop stays short and the database does what it is good at.
8-7g Advantages of Cursors
Cursors buy you real things:

items: A procedure can process an unknown number of rows, from zero to thousands, with the same code.
Each row can take a different path: an IF on the fetched values can write to one table or another, skip a row, or call a different procedure per row.
Values from the row are held in variables, so you can carry a running total, compare this row with the previous one, or build a message that names the customer.
Row-level error handling becomes possible: a handler can log the one row that failed and let the loop continue with the rest.
The work happens inside the database. A caller sends one CALL instead of pulling every row across the network and looping in application code.

blocks.text: Now the honest caution. A cursor loop is still a loop, and SQL is at its best when it operates on a whole set at once. The `REP_CREDIT_REVIEW` procedure above is a fine teaching example and a poor production design, because the rule it applies is expressible in plain SQL. The two `INSERT ... SELECT` statements in the sandbox below produce the same `CUST_REVIEW` contents that the entire loop produced, and because they are ordinary SQL the whole script runs here:

blocks.starter:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS CUST_REVIEW;

CREATE TABLE CUST_REVIEW
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),
     AVAILABLE_CREDIT DECIMAL(9,2),
     REVIEW_NOTE VARCHAR(10));

INSERT INTO CUST_REVIEW
       (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, AVAILABLE_CREDIT, REVIEW_NOTE)
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE, 'Call rep'
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20' AND CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE < 5000;

INSERT INTO CUST_REVIEW
       (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, AVAILABLE_CREDIT, REVIEW_NOTE)
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE, 'No action'
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20' AND CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE >= 5000;

SELECT * FROM CUST_REVIEW ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS CUST_REVIEW;

-- Somewhere for the results to go, exactly as the cursor version used.
CREATE TABLE CUST_REVIEW
    (CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
     CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35),
     AVAILABLE_CREDIT DECIMAL(9,2),
     REVIEW_NOTE VARCHAR(10));

-- The whole cursor loop, replaced by two set-based INSERTs. This one writes the
-- rows that would have taken the IF branch...
INSERT INTO CUST_REVIEW
       (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, AVAILABLE_CREDIT, REVIEW_NOTE)
-- The literal in the SELECT list supplies the same value on every row it writes.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE, 'Call rep'
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20' AND CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE < 5000;

-- ...and this one writes the rows that would have taken the ELSE branch. The
-- two WHERE clauses are the IF, turned inside out.
INSERT INTO CUST_REVIEW
       (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, AVAILABLE_CREDIT, REVIEW_NOTE)
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE, 'No action'
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20' AND CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE >= 5000;

-- Same result as the cursor, in two statements instead of thirty lines - and far
-- faster, because the database does the looping internally.
SELECT * FROM CUST_REVIEW ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.label: Set-based first
blocks.text: With four customers the difference is invisible. With four hundred thousand it is not. A cursor pays per-row overhead on every FETCH and holds its result set open for the life of the loop, which means locks and memory held longer. The optimizer can plan one INSERT ... SELECT as a single operation; it cannot optimize across the iterations of your loop. Write the set-based statement first, and reach for a cursor only when the set-based statement cannot express the work.

cards.title: A cursor earns its place when
cards.body: Each row needs a decision that SQL cannot express in one statement: calling another procedure per row, writing to a different table depending on the values, walking rows in order to carry state from one row to the next, or logging and skipping individual failures while the rest continue.

cards.title: Stay set-based when
cards.body: The rule is a filter, a calculation, or a conditional value that a WHERE clause or a pair of statements can express. UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT ... SELECT already operate on every matching row. If your loop body is one INSERT with no per-row branching, the loop is doing nothing the engine could not do faster.

items: `SELECT ... INTO` requires exactly one row; more than one raises error 1172.
Declare in order: variables, then cursors, then handlers, all at the top of the BEGIN block.
`OPEN` runs the query and positions above the first row; opening it twice raises error 1325.
`FETCH` copies one row into a variable list that matches the cursor's columns in count, order, and type.
`DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;` gives the loop its exit signal.
Test the flag on the line right after the FETCH, before using any fetched value.
`LEAVE` the labelled loop, then `CLOSE` the cursor; closing a cursor that is not open raises error 1326.
Put joins, filters, calculations, and ORDER BY in the cursor query; keep the loop body small.
Before writing a cursor, ask whether one set-based statement would do the same job faster.

questions.scenarioTitle: Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic in one review
questions.stem: A KimTay procedure must review every customer assigned to rep 20, which in the current data means Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. The developer writes `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, BALANCE INTO v_customer_num, v_balance FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num;` and calls the procedure with '20'. What happens, and what belongs there instead?
options: It works, because SELECT INTO repeats itself automatically for every row the WHERE clause matches
It returns Access Pet Center only, so adding an ORDER BY clause makes the procedure correct
The procedure fails with error 1172, so declare a cursor and FETCH the rows one at a time
It stores both customer names in one variable, so a wider VARCHAR declaration fixes the problem
optionNotes: SELECT INTO has no loop of its own; it assigns one row's values one time and then stops
ORDER BY changes the order of rows, never the count, so the two-row result is unchanged
Correct: more than one row breaks SELECT INTO, and a cursor hands the loop one row per FETCH
A variable holds one value; the problem is the number of rows returned, not the width of a column
questions.takeaway: SELECT INTO is a one-row tool, so the moment a query can match many rows the procedure needs a cursor.

questions.scenarioTitle: Compiling the Companion Care Clinic report procedure
questions.stem: A procedure for the KimTay credit report declares the NOT FOUND handler first, then the cursor over CUSTOMER, then the local variables. MySQL refuses to create it. Which arrangement inside BEGIN does MySQL require?
options: Variables and conditions first, then cursor declarations, then handler declarations, then the executable statements
Handlers first, then cursors, then variables, because a handler must exist before anything can go wrong
Any order works as long as every DECLARE appears somewhere inside the BEGIN and END block
Cursors first, then variables, because the cursor query determines which variables the FETCH needs
optionNotes: Correct: MySQL enforces this exact sequence, and a misplaced DECLARE is a compile-time error
The handler is declared last even though it can fire at the first FETCH; declaration order is not run order
MySQL is strict here, and it also requires every DECLARE to precede the first executable statement
The FETCH variable list does depend on the cursor query, but the declarations still go variables first
questions.takeaway: Declaration order in a MySQL block is a syntax rule: variables and conditions, then cursors, then handlers.

questions.scenarioTitle: Whiskers & Wags Boutique logged twice
questions.stem: A cursor loop over invoice lines does its INSERT into the log table first and tests `IF v_done = 1 THEN LEAVE line_loop; END IF;` at the very bottom of the loop body. The log ends up with an extra copy of the last line for Whiskers & Wags Boutique. Why?
options: Nothing is wrong with the loop; the extra row means the cursor query is missing a join condition
The first row is skipped and re-read, because FETCH starts one row below the top of the result set
The NOT FOUND condition is raised as a fatal error, because a CONTINUE handler cannot end a loop
The FETCH that ran out of rows left the previous values in the variables, so they were inserted again
optionNotes: The join is fine; the duplicate comes from the loop structure, which processes one iteration too many
FETCH begins above the first row and the first FETCH retrieves it, so no row is skipped or repeated there
A CONTINUE handler is the right choice; it sets the flag and lets the next statement run normally
Correct: a failed FETCH does not clear the variables, so work done before the flag test repeats the last row
questions.takeaway: Test the done flag on the line immediately after FETCH, before any statement uses the fetched values.

questions.scenarioTitle: Walking Downtown Aquarium & Pets invoice lines
questions.stem: A developer is tracing a cursor procedure that reports the lines on invoice 50712 for Downtown Aquarium & Pets. Which statement actually executes the cursor's SELECT, and which one moves values into the local variables?
options: DECLARE executes the SELECT, and OPEN copies the first row into the variables before the loop starts
OPEN executes the SELECT and positions above the first row; FETCH copies one row into the variables
FETCH executes the SELECT on every call, which is the reason cursor loops are slower than one statement
CLOSE executes the SELECT in reverse order so the same result set can be walked a second time
optionNotes: DECLARE only records the cursor definition; no rows exist until the cursor is opened
Correct: OPEN runs the query once and sets the position, and each FETCH advances one row and assigns variables
FETCH advances through a result set that already exists; it does not re-run the query each time
CLOSE releases the result set; walking the rows again requires a second OPEN after the CLOSE
questions.takeaway: DECLARE defines, OPEN runs the query and positions the cursor, FETCH assigns one row, CLOSE releases it.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's nightly available-credit run
questions.stem: A cursor procedure loops over every KimTay customer, computes `CREDIT_LIMIT - BALANCE`, and inserts one row per customer into a review table with a fixed note. There is no other per-row logic, and the customer table has grown large. What should the DBA do?
options: Replace the loop with set-based INSERT ... SELECT statements, since the loop adds overhead without adding logic
Keep the cursor, because a row-at-a-time loop always uses less memory than a single statement would
Keep the cursor, because an INSERT statement cannot take its values from a SELECT in one statement
Replace the procedure with a view, because a view writes the reviewed rows into the table each night
optionNotes: Correct: with no per-row branching, one INSERT ... SELECT does the same work as a single optimized operation
An open cursor holds its result set and its locks for the whole loop, which is not the cheaper option here
INSERT ... SELECT is standard SQL and is exactly the replacement this workload calls for
A view stores a query, not data, and selecting from it never writes rows into another table
questions.takeaway: Use a cursor only when a row needs a decision SQL cannot express; otherwise the set-based statement wins.

matchers.heading: Sort the cursor lifecycle
matchers.prompt: Each card is a line of code or an event from the KimTay credit-review procedure. Drop it into the stage of the cursor lifecycle it belongs to.

cards.text: DECLARE cust_cursor CURSOR FOR SELECT ... FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = i_rep_num;

cards.text: DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET v_done = 1;
cards.why: The handler must be declared last among the declarations, before any executable statement runs.

cards.text: OPEN cust_cursor;
cards.why: This is the statement that executes the cursor's SELECT and builds the result set.

cards.text: The result set is built and the position is set just above the first customer row

cards.text: FETCH cust_cursor INTO v_customer_num, v_customer_name, v_balance, v_credit_limit;

cards.text: IF v_done = 1 THEN LEAVE cust_loop; END IF;

cards.text: CLOSE cust_cursor;
cards.why: This runs once after the loop has been left and frees the rows the cursor was holding.

cards.text: The cursor name becomes available to be opened again
cards.why: Only after the result set is released can the same cursor be opened for a second pass.

8-8a Error Handling in PL/SQL

Here is the MySQL procedure again, so the comparison is in front of you rather than in your memory. It takes a customer number, reads that customer's name and balance into two local variables, and prints them.

-- MySQL, for comparison with the Oracle and SQL Server versions below.
DELIMITER //

-- CREATE PROCEDURE: MySQL puts the direction (IN) BEFORE the parameter name.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER (IN I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4))
BEGIN

    -- DECLARE, with the type written out in full.
    DECLARE L_NAME    VARCHAR(35);
    DECLARE L_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2);

    -- SELECT ... INTO fills the two locals.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    INTO   L_NAME, L_BALANCE
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- MySQL has no print statement, so output is produced by SELECTing the
    --   variables - the result comes back as a one-row result set.
    SELECT L_NAME AS CUSTOMER_NAME, L_BALANCE AS BALANCE;
END //
DELIMITER ;

That procedure is correct for the case it was written for, which is a customer number that exists and identifies exactly one row. It is silent about the two cases that will eventually happen: somebody passes a number that is not in the table, and somebody changes the `WHERE` clause so more than one row qualifies. Oracle refuses to be silent about either.

-- Oracle PL/SQL. CREATE OR REPLACE: no separate DROP is needed - this replaces
--   any existing procedure of the same name in one statement.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER (I_CUSTOMER_NUM IN CHAR) AS

    -- %TYPE: declare the variable as "whatever type that column is". If the
    --   column is widened later, the variable follows automatically. Note there
    --   is no DECLARE keyword here - in Oracle, declarations simply sit between
    --   AS and BEGIN. Oracle also puts the direction AFTER the parameter name.
    L_NAME     CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE;
    L_BALANCE  CUSTOMER.BALANCE%TYPE;
BEGIN

    -- SELECT ... INTO works the same way as in MySQL.
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    INTO   L_NAME, L_BALANCE
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE: Oracle's print. || joins strings, and TO_CHAR formats
    --   the number to a fixed picture so columns line up.
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(L_NAME || '  ' || TO_CHAR(L_BALANCE, '99999.99'));

-- EXCEPTION: Oracle's error handling is a block at the END of the procedure,
--   rather than handlers declared at the top as in MySQL.
EXCEPTION

    -- NO_DATA_FOUND: the named condition for a SELECT ... INTO that matched
    --   nothing - Oracle's equivalent of MySQL's NOT FOUND.
    WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('No customer numbered ' || I_CUSTOMER_NUM);

    -- TOO_MANY_ROWS: the opposite failure - the INTO matched more than one row.
    --   Oracle gives this its own name; MySQL lumps it under SQLEXCEPTION.
    WHEN TOO_MANY_ROWS THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('That condition matched more than one customer.');

    -- WHEN OTHERS: the catch-all, and it must come last. SQLERRM holds the text
    --   of whatever actually went wrong.
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('Unexpected error: ' || SQLERRM);
END;

-- The lone / on its own line is what tells SQL*Plus to send the block to the
--   server - Oracle's equivalent of MySQL's DELIMITER dance.
/

Everything above the word `EXCEPTION` is the happy path. Everything below it is what to do instead when the happy path fails. Oracle calls a failure an exception, and it hands you three named ones for free. `NO_DATA_FOUND` means the `SELECT ... INTO` matched zero rows. `TOO_MANY_ROWS` means it matched two or more. `OTHERS` means anything else at all, and `SQLERRM` is the message Oracle would have printed if you had not caught it.

blocks.label: Exception
blocks.text: A named run-time failure. In PL/SQL an exception stops the normal flow of a block at the statement that caused it and jumps straight to the block's `EXCEPTION` section, skipping every statement in between. If the block has no matching handler, the exception is passed back to whatever called the block.

The two failure cases are shapes of a result set, not exotic events, and you can watch all three shapes in SQLite even though SQLite does not name them. Run the box below. The first query returns one row, which is the case `GET_CUSTOMER` was written for. The second returns none, which is `NO_DATA_FOUND`. The third returns two, which is `TOO_MANY_ROWS`.

blocks.starter:
-- Case 1: exactly one row comes back. This is the case the procedure was written for.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1225';

-- Case 2: no row comes back. In PL/SQL this raises NO_DATA_FOUND.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1999';

-- Case 3: two rows come back. In PL/SQL this raises TOO_MANY_ROWS.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20';

-- Case 1: exactly one row comes back. This is the case the procedure was written for.
-- Filtering on the PRIMARY KEY is what guarantees at most one row.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1225';

-- Case 2: no row comes back. In PL/SQL this raises NO_DATA_FOUND.
-- The key is valid in shape but matches nothing, and an empty result is not an
-- error to SQL - only to a procedure that expected to fill a variable.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1999';

-- Case 3: two rows come back. In PL/SQL this raises TOO_MANY_ROWS.
-- The difference is the column: REP_NUM is not a key, so it can match many rows,
-- and SELECT ... INTO has no way to choose between them.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20';
blocks.hint: Three queries, three shapes of answer: one row, no rows, two rows. SQLite reports all three as ordinary results. Oracle gives the last two names and expects you to handle them. Case 2 shows an empty area rather than a table, because no row qualified.

blocks.label: Why `%TYPE` is worth the extra typing
blocks.text: `L_NAME CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME%TYPE;` means "whatever type `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME` is declared as, give me one of those." If someone widens that column next year, your procedure follows along without being edited. Writing `L_NAME VARCHAR2(35);` instead pins a copy of today's decision into your code, and copies drift.
Raising an exception of your own

The three built-in exceptions cover mistakes the database can detect. They cannot cover a rule that exists only in KimTay's head, such as never letting a balance climb past its credit limit. For a rule like that you declare an exception, raise it yourself, and handle it in the same section as the built-in ones.

-- Oracle PL/SQL: a procedure that changes data and refuses to leave the database
--   in a state it considers invalid.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE ADD_TO_BALANCE (
    I_CUSTOMER_NUM  IN CHAR,
    I_AMOUNT        IN NUMBER) AS

    -- Declaring your OWN exception. It is not an error the database raises - it
    --   is a name for a business rule you are about to enforce yourself.
    OVER_LIMIT   EXCEPTION;

    -- Two locals typed from the columns they will hold.
    L_BALANCE    CUSTOMER.BALANCE%TYPE;
    L_LIMIT      CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT%TYPE;
BEGIN

    -- The change is made first, then checked. Everything is inside a transaction
    --   until COMMIT, so it can still be taken back.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + I_AMOUNT
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- SQL%ROWCOUNT: how many rows the last statement affected. Zero means the
    --   customer number was wrong - an UPDATE that matches nothing is not an
    --   error, so you have to detect it yourself.
    IF SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 THEN

        -- RAISE: trigger a condition deliberately, sending control to the
        --   EXCEPTION block below.
        RAISE NO_DATA_FOUND;
    END IF;

    -- Read the row back to see what the update actually produced.
    SELECT BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT
    INTO   L_BALANCE, L_LIMIT
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- The business rule. Nothing in the database forbids this, so the procedure
    --   enforces it.
    IF L_BALANCE > L_LIMIT THEN
        RAISE OVER_LIMIT;
    END IF;

    -- COMMIT: reached only when both checks passed. Until this line, nothing is
    --   permanent.
    COMMIT;
EXCEPTION

    -- Every handler rolls back first, so a rejected change leaves no trace.
    WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN
        ROLLBACK;

        -- RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR: hands a numbered error and a readable message
        --   back to the calling program. Numbers from -20000 to -20999 are
        --   reserved for your own application errors.
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20001,
            'No customer numbered ' || I_CUSTOMER_NUM);

    -- The custom exception declared at the top is caught by name here.
    WHEN OVER_LIMIT THEN
        ROLLBACK;
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20002,
            'That charge would push the balance past the credit limit.');

    -- The catch-all for anything unforeseen, still rolling back.
    WHEN OTHERS THEN
        ROLLBACK;
        RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20003, 'Unexpected error: ' || SQLERRM);
END;
/

Notice the order of events. The `UPDATE` runs first, then the check, then `COMMIT`. That is deliberate. Because nothing has been committed when `OVER_LIMIT` is raised, the `ROLLBACK` in the handler puts the balance back exactly as it was. This is the transaction discipline from Module 6, now living inside a procedure instead of inside a session.

blocks.label: `WHEN OTHERS` goes last, always
blocks.text: PL/SQL tries the handlers in the order you wrote them and stops at the first one that matches. `WHEN OTHERS` matches everything, so any handler placed after it is unreachable. If you put `WHEN OTHERS` first, your careful `NO_DATA_FOUND` message never prints and every failure looks the same. Numbers passed to `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` must fall between -20000 and -20999; those are the ones Oracle reserves for you.
8-8b Writing a Complete Procedure Using a Cursor in PL/SQL

A `SELECT ... INTO` handles one row. When the answer is a list, you need a cursor: a name for a query that the procedure can walk through one row at a time, doing whatever it likes at each stop. The task here is the one you wrote in MySQL: given a rep number, list that rep's customers.
The query underneath the cursor is nothing special, and you can run it right now. This is the exact `SELECT` that the PL/SQL cursor below is built on, and rep 20 is Valerie Kaiser's record.

SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- lives inside a procedure - only where the text is kept changes.

FROM CUSTOMER
-- In the procedure this literal is replaced by a parameter, which is the whole
-- point: one stored query answering the question for any rep.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

items.title: Declare
items.body: `CURSOR CUSTGROUP IS ...` names the query. Nothing runs yet. The parameter `I_REP_NUM` is allowed inside the cursor's `WHERE` clause, which is what makes one cursor serve every rep.

items.title: Open
items.body: `OPEN CUSTGROUP;` runs the query and positions the cursor just before the first row. This is the moment the database actually does the work.

items.title: Fetch
items.body: `FETCH CUSTGROUP INTO ...` copies the current row into your three variables and steps forward one row. The variables must match the `SELECT` list in number, order, and type.

items.title: Exit
items.body: `EXIT WHEN CUSTGROUP%NOTFOUND;` is tested immediately after the `FETCH`. `%NOTFOUND` turns true on the fetch that ran off the end, so put this line directly under the `FETCH` and above the work, or you will process the last row twice.

items.title: Close
items.body: `CLOSE CUSTGROUP;` releases the cursor. The handler closes it too, because a block that fails halfway leaves the cursor open otherwise.

blocks.text: For a loop that does nothing but read every row, PL/SQL offers a shorter form that declares the cursor, opens it, fetches, tests, and closes it for you. There are no local variables to declare and no way to forget `CLOSE`.

-- Oracle PL/SQL: the same listing, written the way Oracle programmers actually
--   write it.
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST (I_REP_NUM IN CHAR) AS
BEGIN

    -- FOR ... IN (query) LOOP: a cursor FOR loop. Oracle declares the cursor,
    --   opens it, declares a record to hold each row, fetches, tests for the end
    --   and closes it - all implicitly. Compare it with the version above: the
    --   same job, with every place a mistake could hide taken away.
    FOR C IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
              FROM   CUSTOMER
              WHERE  REP_NUM = I_REP_NUM
              ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM)
    LOOP

        -- C is the loop record, and its fields are named after the query's
        --   columns. Nothing had to be declared for it.
        DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(C.CUSTOMER_NUM || '  ' || C.CUSTOMER_NAME);
    END LOOP;
END;
/

`C` is a record with one field per column in the `SELECT` list, so you write `C.CUSTOMER_NAME` instead of a separately declared variable. Use the long form when you need to do something unusual, such as reading two cursors in step with each other. Use this form the rest of the time.

blocks.label: Seeing the output at all
blocks.text: `DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE` writes to a buffer, not to your screen. In SQL*Plus and SQL Developer you have to ask for that buffer to be displayed, once per session, with `SET SERVEROUTPUT ON;`. A procedure that appears to print nothing is very often a procedure that ran perfectly into a buffer nobody read.

cards.title: What travels between engines
cards.body: A procedure is a named, stored, parameterised block of logic. A cursor is opened, fetched from in a loop, and closed. A failure is trapped in one place rather than checked after every statement. Learn these three and you can read procedural code in any of the engines in this module.

cards.title: What does not travel
cards.body: Where you declare variables, how you end the block, how you print, and what the failure cases are called. Oracle names `NO_DATA_FOUND` and `TOO_MANY_ROWS`; MySQL and SQL Server do not. Never paste a PL/SQL block into a different engine and expect a small edit to fix it.

items: Declare local variables above `BEGIN`, not inside the body, and prefer `%TYPE` over a hand-copied data type.
Put `EXCEPTION` after the last statement of the happy path and before `END;`.
List `WHEN OTHERS` last, because it matches everything ahead of any handler placed after it.
Test `%NOTFOUND` immediately after the `FETCH` and before you use the fetched values.
Close the cursor in the handler as well as at the end of the happy path.
Turn on `SET SERVEROUTPUT ON;` before you decide your procedure printed nothing.

blocks.text: Third dialect, same five tasks. Microsoft SQL Server's procedural language is Transact-SQL, universally shortened to T-SQL. It reaches the same destinations as MySQL and PL/SQL and takes a visibly different road: every local variable name starts with `@`, you assign to a variable inside the `SELECT` list rather than with `INTO`, and there is no `EXCEPTION` keyword because errors are trapped with `BEGIN TRY` and `BEGIN CATCH`.

One row of this table matters more than the rest. Read the fourth row twice. T-SQL's `SELECT @L_VAR = col` does not object when the query matches the wrong number of rows, which means the safety net Oracle gave you for free is a net you have to weave yourself.

8-9a Retrieving a Single Row and Column in T-SQL
Same task as 8-8a: given a customer number, report that customer's name and balance.

-- SQL Server T-SQL. CREATE PROCEDURE with no parentheses around the parameter
--   list, and every parameter and variable name starting with @.
CREATE PROCEDURE GET_CUSTOMER
    @I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4)

-- AS: opens the body. T-SQL does not require BEGIN ... END around it.
AS

-- DECLARE: the @ prefix is part of the name here, not a marker for something
--   special as it is in MySQL.
DECLARE @L_NAME    VARCHAR(35);
DECLARE @L_BALANCE DECIMAL(9,2);
DECLARE @L_ROWS    INT;

-- SELECT @variable = column: T-SQL's way of loading variables from a query -
--   assignments inside the SELECT list, with no INTO clause at all.
SELECT @L_NAME    = CUSTOMER_NAME,
       @L_BALANCE = BALANCE
FROM   CUSTOMER
WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- @@ROWCOUNT: how many rows the previous statement touched. Capture it
--   immediately - the very next statement overwrites it.
SET @L_ROWS = @@ROWCOUNT;

-- T-SQL raises nothing when this SELECT matches no row, so the procedure has to
--   test the count itself. Zero rows means no such customer.
IF @L_ROWS = 0

    -- PRINT: T-SQL's print statement. + joins strings here, where Oracle used ||.
    PRINT 'No customer numbered ' + @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- More than one row means the variables hold the LAST row read, silently.
ELSE IF @L_ROWS > 1
    PRINT 'That condition matched more than one customer.';

-- Exactly one row: the normal path.
ELSE

    -- CAST is required, because T-SQL will not join a number to a string.
    PRINT @L_NAME + '  ' + CAST(@L_BALANCE AS VARCHAR(20));

-- GO: not SQL at all, but a batch separator the client uses to decide where one
--   piece of work ends. It plays the same role as MySQL's DELIMITER and Oracle's /.
GO

The `IF` block is not decoration. Without it, a customer number that is not in `CUSTOMER` leaves `@L_NAME` holding whatever it held before, which is `NULL` on the first call and yesterday's customer on a later one. A condition matching two rows leaves `@L_NAME` holding the last row the query happened to return, in whatever order the engine chose. Neither case raises anything.

`@@ROWCOUNT` is how you find out, and it is a moving target: every statement resets it, including an `IF` that does nothing but test it. That is why the procedure copies it into `@L_ROWS` on the very next line and then tests `@L_ROWS` twice. Written the tempting way, as `IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 ... ELSE IF @@ROWCOUNT > 1`, the second test would be reading the count left behind by the first `IF` rather than the count from the `SELECT`, and the two-row case would never be reported.

blocks.label: The single most portable-looking difference that is not portable
blocks.text: `SELECT ... INTO` means two completely different things. In MySQL and Oracle it copies column values into local variables. In T-SQL, `SELECT col INTO NEW_TABLE FROM ...` creates a brand-new table and fills it, which is the `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` behaviour from 6-1. Assigning to a T-SQL variable is always `SELECT @var = col` or `SET @var = (SELECT ...)`.

blocks.solution:
-- The single-row lookup a procedure would perform with SELECT ... INTO. Filtering
-- on the primary key is what makes it safe: at most one row can ever come back.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1420';

Change 1420 to 1999 and the box shows an empty result, which is the case the @@ROWCOUNT test is there to catch.

blocks.text: 8-9b Changing Data with a Stored Procedure in T-SQL

Reading is the easy half. A procedure that changes data has to decide what to do when the change does not apply, and it has to leave the database in a sane state when something fails halfway. Here is a procedure that adds an amount to a customer's balance, refuses to touch a customer number that does not exist, and rolls back rather than committing a half-finished change.

-- SQL Server T-SQL: a data change wrapped in a transaction with structured
--   error handling.
CREATE PROCEDURE ADD_TO_BALANCE
    @I_CUSTOMER_NUM CHAR(4),
    @I_AMOUNT       DECIMAL(9,2)
AS

-- BEGIN TRY: everything up to END TRY is protected. If any statement inside
--   fails, control jumps straight to the CATCH block.
BEGIN TRY

    -- Open the transaction so a failure can be undone.
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;

    -- The change itself.
    UPDATE CUSTOMER
    SET    BALANCE = BALANCE + @I_AMOUNT
    WHERE  CUSTOMER_NUM = @I_CUSTOMER_NUM;

    -- An UPDATE that matched nothing is not an error, so check the count and
    --   turn it into one deliberately.
    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0

        -- THROW: raise an error with your own number and message. Anything from
        --   50000 up is yours to use. This sends control to CATCH.
        THROW 50001, 'No customer with that number. Nothing was changed.', 1;

    -- Reached only when the update touched a row.
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY

-- BEGIN CATCH: runs only when something in the TRY block failed.
BEGIN CATCH

    -- @@TRANCOUNT: how many transactions are open. Test it before rolling back -
    --   a ROLLBACK with no open transaction is itself an error.
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

    -- ERROR_MESSAGE(): the text of whatever went wrong, available only inside a
    --   CATCH block.
    PRINT 'ADD_TO_BALANCE failed: ' + ERROR_MESSAGE();
END CATCH;
GO

Here `@@ROWCOUNT` is read once, on the statement immediately after the `UPDATE`, so it needs no variable. `THROW` raises an error, which sends control straight to `BEGIN CATCH`, exactly the way `RAISE` sends a PL/SQL block to its `EXCEPTION` section. Numbers at or above 50000 are the ones reserved for your own errors. `@@TRANCOUNT` is checked before the rollback because a `ROLLBACK` with no open transaction is itself an error, and an error inside a `CATCH` block has nowhere left to go.
