blocks.text: 8-9c Deleting Data with a Stored Procedure in T-SQL

A delete procedure has the same shape and one extra hazard. A row that other rows still point at cannot be deleted, and the database will say so. That is the foreign key doing its job, and a procedure that ignores the possibility will hand a raw engine error to whoever called it.

-- SQL Server T-SQL: a delete that reports all three of its possible outcomes.
CREATE PROCEDURE DELETE_ITEM
    @I_ITEM_ID CHAR(4)
AS
BEGIN TRY

    -- The delete, with its WHERE clause built into the procedure.
    DELETE FROM ITEM
    WHERE  ITEM_ID = @I_ITEM_ID;

    -- Outcome 1: nothing matched. Not an error, so it is detected by the count.
    IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0
        PRINT 'No item numbered ' + @I_ITEM_ID + '. Nothing was deleted.';

    -- Outcome 2: the row was removed.
    ELSE
        PRINT 'Item ' + @I_ITEM_ID + ' deleted.';
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH

    -- Outcome 3: the delete was refused - typically by a foreign key, because
    --   invoice lines still point at the item. ERROR_MESSAGE() reports which.
    PRINT 'Could not delete ' + @I_ITEM_ID + ': ' + ERROR_MESSAGE();
END CATCH;
GO

`DG04` is the Nylon Dog Leash, and invoice 50710 still lists it. SQL Server refuses the delete, `CATCH` receives control, and the caller gets a sentence in English instead of a stack trace. Note the two distinct outcomes the procedure now distinguishes: an item that could not be deleted, and an item that was never there. Those are different problems and they deserve different messages.

This page's engine will enforce the same rule if you ask it to. `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` turns enforcement on for the session, and then the delete below fails with `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`. That statement is shown rather than run because the error would replace everything else in the output.

-- PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON: SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless you ask
--   it to, and the setting lasts only for this connection.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

-- DELETE: the same attempt, in the sandbox on this page. INVOICE_LINE holds rows
--   referring to DG04, so the delete is refused and you see the error the SQL
--   Server CATCH block above was reporting.
DELETE FROM ITEM
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

blocks.solution:
-- Step 1: find out what still points at DG04.
-- This is the query behind the error message: these are the rows a foreign key
-- would be protecting if the delete were attempted.
SELECT INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED
FROM INVOICE_LINE
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

-- Step 2: delete it from a working copy, where no foreign key is watching.
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ITEM_WORK;
-- CREATE TABLE ... AS copies the columns and rows but NOT the constraints, which
-- is exactly why the delete below is allowed to succeed here.
CREATE TABLE ITEM_WORK AS SELECT * FROM ITEM;

DELETE FROM ITEM_WORK
WHERE ITEM_ID = 'DG04';

-- Four rows in the copy, five still in the real ITEM table.

FROM ITEM_WORK
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;

blocks.text: 8-9d Using a Cursor in T-SQL
Same task as 8-8b: list one rep's customers, one row at a time. T-SQL cursors have four moving parts that PL/SQL hides, and all four have to be right.

-- SQL Server T-SQL: the cursor loop, third dialect.
CREATE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST
    @I_REP_NUM CHAR(2)
AS

-- One variable per cursor column, all declared up front.
DECLARE @L_CUSTOMER_NUM  CHAR(4);
DECLARE @L_CUSTOMER_NAME VARCHAR(35);
DECLARE @L_BALANCE       DECIMAL(9,2);

-- DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR: the query to be walked.
DECLARE CUSTGROUP CURSOR FOR
    SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE
    FROM   CUSTOMER
    WHERE  REP_NUM = @I_REP_NUM
    ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- Run the query and get ready to read.
OPEN CUSTGROUP;

-- FETCH NEXT FROM ... INTO: T-SQL spells out the direction. The FIRST fetch
--   happens BEFORE the loop - that is what makes a WHILE loop possible here.
FETCH NEXT FROM CUSTGROUP
    INTO @L_CUSTOMER_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_BALANCE;

-- @@FETCH_STATUS: 0 means the last fetch worked. Testing it at the TOP of the
--   loop replaces MySQL's flag-and-handler arrangement entirely.
WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0
BEGIN

    -- The work for this row.
    PRINT @L_CUSTOMER_NUM + '  ' + @L_CUSTOMER_NAME + '  ' +
          CAST(@L_BALANCE AS VARCHAR(20));

    -- The SECOND fetch, at the bottom of the loop. Forget this line and the
    --   loop repeats the same row forever - the classic T-SQL cursor bug.
    FETCH NEXT FROM CUSTGROUP
        INTO @L_CUSTOMER_NUM, @L_CUSTOMER_NAME, @L_BALANCE;
END

-- CLOSE releases the rows...
CLOSE CUSTGROUP;

-- ...and DEALLOCATE releases the cursor's name. T-SQL needs both; MySQL and
--   Oracle need only the close.
DEALLOCATE CUSTGROUP;
GO

items.title: The priming fetch
items.body: The `FETCH NEXT` above the `WHILE` exists so that `@@FETCH_STATUS` has a value the first time the loop condition is tested. Without it the loop is testing the status of some earlier, unrelated fetch.

items.title: The fetch at the bottom
items.body: The second `FETCH NEXT` is the last statement inside the loop. Leave it out and `@@FETCH_STATUS` never changes, the condition stays true, and the procedure prints the first customer forever.

items.title: `@@FETCH_STATUS` is global
items.body: It reports on the most recent fetch on any cursor in the session, not on `CUSTGROUP` specifically. Test it immediately after the fetch you care about, before any other statement can overwrite it.

items.title: `CLOSE` then `DEALLOCATE`
items.body: `CLOSE` releases the rows. `DEALLOCATE` releases the name, so `CUSTGROUP` can be declared again. Skip `DEALLOCATE` and the second call to the procedure fails with a complaint that a cursor with that name already exists.

blocks.label: Reach for a set before you reach for a cursor
blocks.text: A cursor processes one row per trip through the loop. A single `UPDATE` or `SELECT` processes all the matching rows in one statement, and the engine is free to optimise it. Write a cursor when each row needs its own decision that SQL cannot express, and not because looping feels more familiar than thinking in sets.

blocks.text: A cursor that changes the row it is sitting on
Declaring a cursor `FOR UPDATE OF` a column lets the loop modify the row it has just fetched, using `WHERE CURRENT OF` instead of a `WHERE` clause that has to find the row all over again.

That loop touches the two Habitat items, `AV07` and `FT88`, and adds 10 to each. It is also a good example of a cursor that should not have been written, because one `UPDATE ITEM SET ON_HAND = ON_HAND + 10 WHERE CATEGORY = 'Habitat';` does the identical job in a single statement. Reserve `WHERE CURRENT OF` for the case where the new value depends on a decision you can only make row by row.

blocks.label: Declaring the cursor honestly makes it cheaper
blocks.text: `DECLARE LINEGROUP CURSOR LOCAL FAST_FORWARD FOR ...` tells SQL Server the cursor is read-only, moves forward only, and is not visible outside the routine that declared it. That is what most reporting cursors actually are, and saying so lets the engine skip the machinery a scrollable, updatable cursor needs. Do not add `FOR UPDATE OF` to a cursor that never updates anything.

items: Every local variable name begins with `@`, and so does every parameter.
Assign with `SELECT @var = col`, never `SELECT col INTO var`, which builds a table in T-SQL.
Read `@@ROWCOUNT` on the statement immediately after the one you are asking about, and copy it into a variable if you need to test it more than once.
Write the priming `FETCH` above the loop and the advancing `FETCH` as the loop's last statement.
End with `CLOSE` and then `DEALLOCATE`, so the cursor name is free for the next call.
Trap failures in `BEGIN CATCH`, and check `@@TRANCOUNT` before rolling anything back.

blocks.text: Everything in 8-8 and 8-9 had to be called. Somebody typed `EXECUTE` or `EXEC` or `CALL`, and the procedure ran. A trigger is the opposite arrangement: it is stored code that nobody calls, attached to a table, that the database itself runs whenever a particular kind of change hits that table. This is the one topic in the module that runs in the sandbox on this page, so you can watch it happen instead of taking it on faith.

blocks.label: Trigger
blocks.text: A block of code stored in the database and attached to one table, which the database executes automatically when a row of that table is inserted, updated, or deleted. It has no name at the call site because there is no call site. The statement that caused it does not mention it and cannot see it.

Triggers exist in all four engines in this module, with the same idea and four different spellings. Two things vary: how you name the row being changed, and whether the trigger runs once per row or once per statement.

blocks.caption: Trigger syntax across the four engines in this module
headers: How it refers to the row
rows: `CREATE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW`, wrapped in `DELIMITER //`
`CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW`
`CREATE TRIGGER n ON t AFTER INSERT AS` -- no `FOR EACH ROW`
The `inserted` and `deleted` tables, holding every affected row at once
`CREATE TRIGGER n AFTER INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW`

blocks.label: The SQL Server row is a real difference, not a spelling difference
blocks.text: MySQL, Oracle and SQLite run a row-level trigger once for every row the statement touched. SQL Server runs the trigger once for the whole statement and hands you two tables, `inserted` and `deleted`, containing all the affected rows. Code written as though `inserted` holds exactly one row is correct until the day somebody inserts two rows in one statement, and then it silently processes only one of them.
An audit log, end to end

KimTay wants a permanent record of every invoice line as it is added: which invoice, which item, how many, and when. Nobody is going to remember to write that second `INSERT` every time, and a rule that depends on everybody remembering is not a rule. Run the box below and watch the log row appear without anything asking for it.

blocks.solution:
-- Housekeeping first, so this whole box can be run more than once.
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS LOG_NEW_LINE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS INVOICE_LINE_LOG;
DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50712' AND ITEM_ID = 'GR15';

-- 1. The audit table. Nothing writes to it by hand, ever.
CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE_LOG (
    -- INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite numbers itself, so the trigger never supplies it.
    LOG_ID       INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    INVOICE_NUM  CHAR(5),
    ITEM_ID      CHAR(4),
    NUM_ORDERED  SMALLINT,
    LOGGED_ON    DATE
);

-- 2. The trigger. It fires after each new INVOICE_LINE row lands.
CREATE TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE
-- The event: after an insert on this table, and only after it succeeds.
AFTER INSERT ON INVOICE_LINE
-- FOR EACH ROW: run the body once per row inserted, not once per statement.
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE_LOG (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, LOGGED_ON)
    -- NEW holds the row being inserted. On an INSERT there is no OLD, because
    -- the row did not exist a moment ago.
    VALUES (NEW.INVOICE_NUM, NEW.ITEM_ID, NEW.NUM_ORDERED, DATE('now'));
END;

-- 3. One ordinary INSERT. Nothing here mentions the log table.
INSERT INTO INVOICE_LINE (INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, QUOTED_PRICE)
VALUES ('50712', 'GR15', 4, 15.25);

-- 4. Proof the trigger ran.
-- Two statements were executed and two rows were written, in two tables.
SELECT LOG_ID, INVOICE_NUM, ITEM_ID, NUM_ORDERED, LOGGED_ON
FROM INVOICE_LINE_LOG;
blocks.hint: One row comes back: 50712, GR15, 4, and whatever date you pressed Run. Read statement 3 again and notice it says nothing about INVOICE_LINE_LOG. That is the whole point of a trigger, and also the whole danger. Delete statement 2, press Run again, and the log comes back empty.

blocks.text: Read statement 3 one more time. It is an ordinary `INSERT` into `INVOICE_LINE`. It does not name `INVOICE_LINE_LOG`, does not know the log exists, and would be written identically by somebody who had never heard of the trigger. The log row appeared anyway, because the database ran the trigger between the row landing and the statement finishing.

blocks.label: Why the box opens with three lines of housekeeping
blocks.text: The sandbox keeps its database between one press of Run and the next. A second `CREATE TABLE INVOICE_LINE_LOG` would fail because the table already exists, a second `CREATE TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE` would fail for the same reason, and a second `INSERT` of the same invoice line would fail on the primary key. `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS`, `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`, and a targeted `DELETE` put the sandbox back to a known state so the box gives the same answer every time.
`OLD` and `NEW`

Inside the trigger body, `NEW` is the row as it will be after the change and `OLD` is the row as it was before. An `INSERT` has a `NEW` and no `OLD`, a `DELETE` has an `OLD` and no `NEW`, and an `UPDATE` has both. That is what makes an update trigger the natural place to record a before-and-after audit trail.

blocks.solution:
-- Housekeeping, including resetting the balance so the box can be re-run.
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS LOG_BALANCE_CHANGE;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS BALANCE_LOG;
UPDATE CUSTOMER SET BALANCE = 3512.50 WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

CREATE TABLE BALANCE_LOG (
    LOG_ID        INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    CUSTOMER_NUM  CHAR(4),
    OLD_BALANCE   DECIMAL(9,2),
    NEW_BALANCE   DECIMAL(9,2)
);

CREATE TRIGGER LOG_BALANCE_CHANGE
-- OF BALANCE narrows the event: changing any other column does not fire this.
AFTER UPDATE OF BALANCE ON CUSTOMER
FOR EACH ROW
-- WHEN adds a condition the row must meet before the body runs. Here it filters
-- out updates that set the balance to the value it already had.
WHEN OLD.BALANCE <> NEW.BALANCE
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO BALANCE_LOG (CUSTOMER_NUM, OLD_BALANCE, NEW_BALANCE)
    -- On an UPDATE both OLD and NEW exist, which is what makes a before-and-after
    -- audit possible.
    VALUES (OLD.CUSTOMER_NUM, OLD.BALANCE, NEW.BALANCE);
END;

-- A real change. This one is logged.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE + 250.00
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- A change that changes nothing. The WHEN clause skips it.
-- The UPDATE still runs and still touches the row; only the trigger body is
-- skipped, which keeps the audit free of no-op entries.
UPDATE CUSTOMER
SET BALANCE = BALANCE
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1120';

-- One row, not two.
SELECT LOG_ID, CUSTOMER_NUM, OLD_BALANCE, NEW_BALANCE
FROM BALANCE_LOG;
blocks.hint: Exactly one log row: 1120, 3512.5, 3762.5. Two UPDATE statements ran but only one was a real change, and the WHEN clause is what kept the second one out of the log. Delete the WHEN line and press Run again to see the noise it was filtering.

blocks.text: Two features are doing work in that trigger. `AFTER UPDATE OF BALANCE` narrows it to updates that name the `BALANCE` column, so an address correction never wakes it up. `WHEN OLD.BALANCE <> NEW.BALANCE` narrows it further to updates that actually moved the number. Without them the log fills with entries recording that nothing happened, and a log nobody trusts is a log nobody reads.
`BEFORE` and `AFTER`
The timing word decides when the trigger runs relative to the change, and that decides what it is capable of.

cards.title: `BEFORE`
cards.body: Runs while the row is still a proposal. The change has not been applied and no other trigger has seen it. This is the timing that can refuse the statement outright, and in some engines it can adjust the incoming values. Use it for validation and normalisation: rules about whether a row is allowed in at all.

cards.title: `AFTER`
cards.body: Runs once the row is on file and every constraint has been satisfied. The change is real, so the trigger can safely act on it: write an audit row, adjust a total in another table, queue a notification. Use it for consequences, meaning things that should follow from a change that has already been accepted.

blocks.text: A `BEFORE` trigger refuses a row by raising an error. On this page the call is `RAISE(ABORT, 'message')`, wrapped in a `SELECT` because SQLite trigger bodies contain statements. Oracle uses `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR`, SQL Server uses `THROW`, MySQL uses `SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'`. All four cancel the statement and hand the message back to whoever wrote it.

blocks.solution:
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS CHECK_CREDIT_LIMIT;
DELETE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1500';

CREATE TRIGGER CHECK_CREDIT_LIMIT
-- BEFORE, not AFTER: the trigger has to run while the insert can still be
-- stopped. An AFTER trigger fires once the row is already in.
BEFORE INSERT ON CUSTOMER
FOR EACH ROW
-- Only rows over the ceiling are worth checking, so WHEN filters the rest out.
WHEN NEW.CREDIT_LIMIT > 10000
BEGIN
    -- RAISE(ABORT, message) cancels the statement and reports your own wording.
    -- This is a business rule enforced in the database rather than in an
    -- application, so it holds no matter which program does the inserting.
    SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'Credit limit over 10000 needs manager approval');
END;

-- Within the ceiling, so this one is stored.
-- The WHEN condition is false, the trigger body never runs, and the insert
-- proceeds exactly as though no trigger existed.
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, STREET, CITY, STATE, ZIP,
                      BALANCE, CREDIT_LIMIT, REP_NUM)
VALUES ('1500', 'Harbor Pet Supply', '12 Dock St.', 'Northfield', 'OH', '44067',
        0.00, 9000.00, '35');

SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CREDIT_LIMIT
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = '1500';
blocks.hint: As written the insert succeeds and Harbor Pet Supply appears with a credit limit of 9000. Now change 9000.00 to 15000.00 and press Run again: the WHEN clause turns true, RAISE(ABORT) cancels the statement, and the box reports the message instead of a table. Nothing was stored, which is what BEFORE buys you.

blocks.text: The cost: effects you cannot see at the call site

A trigger can change a table nobody mentioned. That is genuinely useful and it is also the reason triggers get a bad reputation. Run the box below, then read the two statements in it and try to explain from them alone why `ON_HAND` moved.

blocks.hint: The Small Animal Grooming Kit ends at 18, down from its seeded 22. The INSERT names INVOICE_LINE and only INVOICE_LINE, yet a row in ITEM changed. The UPDATE at the top resets ON_HAND to 22 so the box gives 18 every time rather than 14, then 10, then 6.

blocks.label: A trigger is invisible from the statement that fires it
blocks.text: Somebody debugging that `INSERT` sees one statement touching one table. They will not find the `UPDATE` by reading the application, because it is not in the application. They will not find it by reading the `INSERT`, because it is not there either. Two rules keep this manageable: write down in the schema documentation every trigger you create, and never write a trigger whose job could have been done by a constraint, a default, or a plain statement in the calling code.

There is a second, quieter hazard. A trigger that updates a table which has its own trigger will fire that one too, and a chain of triggers can end up doing far more work than the original statement suggests, or in the worst case circle back to the table it started from. Keep bodies short, keep the chain shallow, and prefer one trigger doing one thing.
Finding and removing triggers

Because a trigger is invisible at the call site, being able to list the ones a database holds is not optional. On this page they live in `sqlite_master` alongside tables, views and indexes. MySQL and SQL Server use `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TRIGGERS`, and Oracle uses `USER_TRIGGERS`.

blocks.hint: One row: LOG_NEW_LINE, trigger, INVOICE_LINE. That third column is the one that matters when you are trying to work out why a table keeps changing on its own. To watch the listing empty out, add DROP TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE; immediately ABOVE the SELECT and press Run again. Putting it after the SELECT changes nothing you can see, because the catalog is read before the drop happens.

blocks.text: `DROP TRIGGER LOG_NEW_LINE;` removes it, in every engine here. Dropping the table a trigger is attached to removes the trigger with it, which is worth knowing before you rebuild a table using the copy-and-rename pattern from 6-8a and wonder later why the audit log went quiet.

items: Choose `BEFORE` to refuse or adjust a row, and `AFTER` to act on a row that has been accepted.
Use `NEW` for the incoming values and `OLD` for the values being replaced; an `INSERT` has no `OLD` and a `DELETE` has no `NEW`.
Narrow the trigger with `UPDATE OF column` and a `WHEN` clause so it does not fire on changes it does not care about.
Write `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS` above `CREATE TRIGGER` in any script you expect to run twice.
In SQL Server, write the body against the `inserted` and `deleted` tables as sets, because it fires once per statement, not once per row.
Document every trigger you create, because nobody will find it by reading the statement that fires it.

blocks.text: This module took one small set of tasks and wrote them out in three procedural dialects: MySQL, Oracle PL/SQL, and SQL Server T-SQL, with the trigger written once more in this page's own SQLite. Fetch one customer's name and balance. Change a balance safely. Delete an item that other rows may still reference. Walk a list one row at a time. Do something automatically when a row arrives. The tasks did not get harder as you moved between engines. Only the spelling changed, and noticing which parts were spelling and which parts were ideas is the actual skill.

Three things are ideas. A stored procedure is named, parameterised logic that lives in the database rather than in an application, so every caller gets the same rules. A cursor is a way to hand a query's rows to your own logic one at a time, for the cases where a single statement cannot express the decision. A trigger is logic the database runs for you, attached to a table rather than to a caller. Those three transfer to any engine you meet.

blocks.caption: The module's tasks in three procedural dialects
rows: `SELECT col INTO L_VAR FROM ...` in both
`DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND` / `WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN`
Trap a failure in one place
`ON t AFTER INSERT`, the `inserted` table, once per statement

items: PL/SQL names its failure cases. `NO_DATA_FOUND` and `TOO_MANY_ROWS` are raised for you; `WHEN OTHERS` catches the rest and must be listed last.
You can declare and raise an exception of your own for a business rule the database cannot know about, and report it with `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` using a number between -20000 and -20999.
T-SQL raises nothing when an assignment matches zero rows or many. `@@ROWCOUNT`, read on the very next statement and copied into a variable if you need to test it more than once, is how you find out.
A T-SQL cursor needs a priming `FETCH` before the loop, an advancing `FETCH` as the loop's last statement, and both `CLOSE` and `DEALLOCATE` at the end.
A cursor is the right tool only when each row needs its own decision. When `SUM`, a single `UPDATE`, or a join can answer the question, they are faster and shorter.
Triggers run without being called. `BEFORE` can refuse a row; `AFTER` acts on a row already accepted. `NEW` and `OLD` name the incoming and outgoing versions.
SQL Server triggers fire once per statement and read the `inserted` and `deleted` tables, so trigger bodies written for one row are quietly wrong for a multi-row statement.
Nothing at the call site reveals that a trigger exists, which is why every trigger belongs in the schema documentation and why a constraint is the better tool whenever one will do.

blocks.label: What this page could and could not show you
blocks.text: Triggers ran here for real, in SQLite, and so did every query underneath the procedures. Stored procedures, PL/SQL, and T-SQL did not, because SQLite implements none of them. That is not a gap in the material; it is the reason the dialect tables exist. When you next sit in front of Oracle or SQL Server, the table for that engine is the translation key, and the ideas underneath it are already yours.

items: I can explain the difference between a stored procedure and a trigger in terms of who calls it.
I can say what `NO_DATA_FOUND` means and name the T-SQL test that does the same job.
I can write a cursor loop in either dialect and say where the loop stops and why.
I can choose between `BEFORE` and `AFTER` for a stated requirement and defend the choice.
I can predict what `OLD` and `NEW` hold for an insert, an update, and a delete.
I can name two reasons a trigger is harder to debug than the same code written in the caller.

questions.scenarioTitle: A customer number KimTay has never issued
questions.stem: KimTay's `GET_CUSTOMER` procedure runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE INTO L_NAME, L_BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM = I_CUSTOMER_NUM;` and is called with '1999', which is not in the table. What does Oracle do next?
options: Raises `NO_DATA_FOUND` and jumps straight to the block's `EXCEPTION` section
Raises `TOO_MANY_ROWS`, because zero rows is not the one row the statement demanded
Leaves both variables unchanged and carries on to the statement after the `SELECT`
Reports a syntax error, because `SELECT ... INTO` cannot appear inside a procedure
optionNotes: Correct. A `SELECT ... INTO` promises exactly one row. Zero rows breaks that promise, and Oracle names the break `NO_DATA_FOUND` so a handler can decide what the caller sees.
`TOO_MANY_ROWS` is the opposite failure: two or more rows matched. Zero and many are different problems with different names and usually different responses.
This is the MySQL habit applied to Oracle. MySQL leaves the variables alone unless you declared a `NOT FOUND` handler; Oracle refuses to continue at all and raises an exception instead.
`SELECT ... INTO` is the normal way a PL/SQL block reads a single row. It is legal inside a procedure and nowhere else in Oracle SQL.
questions.takeaway: In PL/SQL a `SELECT ... INTO` that matches no row raises `NO_DATA_FOUND`; it never quietly leaves the variables as they were.

questions.scenarioTitle: Listing Valerie Kaiser's two customers
questions.stem: `REP_CUSTOMER_LIST` opens a cursor over rep 20's customers and fetches into three variables inside a `LOOP`. What stops the loop after the second customer?
options: `CUSTGROUP%FOUND` turning true, which happens on the first successful `FETCH`
`EXIT WHEN CUSTGROUP%NOTFOUND;`, tested right after the `FETCH` that returned nothing
`CLOSE CUSTGROUP;`, because closing a cursor ends any loop that was reading it
A fixed count of passes equal to the number of rows in `CUSTOMER`, whatever the `WHERE` clause says
optionNotes: `%FOUND` is true while fetches are succeeding, so exiting on it would end the loop before the first customer was printed. It is the attribute you test to continue, not to stop.
Correct. The third `FETCH` runs past the last row, `%NOTFOUND` turns true, and the `EXIT WHEN` immediately below the `FETCH` ends the loop before the stale variable values are used again.
`CLOSE` is written after the loop and cannot run until the loop has already ended. Closing a cursor releases it; it is not a loop-control statement.
The cursor visits only the rows its query returned, which is two here because of `WHERE REP_NUM = I_REP_NUM`. `CUSTOMER` holding four rows is irrelevant.
questions.takeaway: Put `EXIT WHEN cursor%NOTFOUND;` immediately after the `FETCH` and above the work, or the loop processes the last row a second time.

questions.scenarioTitle: A charge that would push Whiskers & Wags past its limit
questions.stem: `ADD_TO_BALANCE` runs the `UPDATE` first, then checks the new balance against `CREDIT_LIMIT` and raises a user-defined `OVER_LIMIT` exception. What must the handler do so KimTay never keeps the over-limit balance?
options: List `WHEN OTHERS` ahead of `WHEN OVER_LIMIT` so the general handler runs first
Leave the handler empty, because PL/SQL undoes every statement in a failed procedure automatically
Roll back the uncommitted `UPDATE`, then report the refusal with `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR`
Re-run the `UPDATE` with a smaller amount until the credit limit is no longer exceeded
optionNotes: Handlers are tried in the order written and `WHEN OTHERS` matches everything, so putting it first makes every handler below it unreachable and every failure look identical.
PL/SQL does not roll back a transaction because a block raised an exception. The `UPDATE` is still sitting uncommitted, and something has to undo it explicitly.
Correct. Nothing was committed, so `ROLLBACK` restores the balance exactly, and `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` with a number in the -20000 to -20999 range tells the caller why in plain words.
A procedure guessing at a smaller amount invents data nobody asked for. The correct response to a refused business rule is to refuse and say so, not to substitute a value.
questions.takeaway: An exception stops the block but does not undo the transaction; roll back inside the handler and report the refusal with `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR`.

quizzes.heading: Check Yourself: T-SQL in SQL Server

questions.scenarioTitle: Two of Valerie Kaiser's customers at once
questions.stem: A T-SQL procedure runs `SELECT @L_NAME = CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20';`. Both Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic match. What ends up in `@L_NAME`?
options: Nothing, because SQL Server raises an error when an assignment matches more than one row
Both names joined by a comma, because the assignment collects every value it matched
The name from whichever row the query returned last, with no warning of any kind
`NULL`, because SQL Server cannot decide which of the two rows was meant
optionNotes: This is Oracle's behaviour, where the same situation raises `TOO_MANY_ROWS`. T-SQL has no equivalent and treats the multi-row case as ordinary.
An assignment stores one value. Combining several rows into one string is something you would have to write deliberately with `STRING_AGG` or similar.

Correct. The assignment is repeated for every matching row, so the last row processed wins, and the order is whatever the engine chose. Capture `@@ROWCOUNT` into a variable on the very next statement if that matters.
Nulling the variable would at least be a visible signal. T-SQL gives you a plausible-looking value from a row you never asked for, which is harder to notice.
questions.takeaway: `SELECT @var = col` silently keeps the last matching row, so save `@@ROWCOUNT` on the next statement whenever exactly one row is required.

questions.scenarioTitle: Walking a rep's customers one at a time
questions.stem: A T-SQL cursor loop is controlled by `WHILE @@FETCH_STATUS = 0`. Why does `FETCH NEXT` appear once above the loop and again as the loop's last statement?
options: The first gives `@@FETCH_STATUS` a value to test; the second advances to the following row
SQL Server requires every cursor to be read twice before it may be closed
The first counts the rows and the second retrieves their values into the variables
One reads forward and the other reads backward so the loop can be restarted
optionNotes: Correct. Without the priming fetch the `WHILE` tests the status of some earlier fetch; without the one inside, the status never changes and the loop repeats the first row forever.
There is no such requirement. The two fetches are there because of how `WHILE` evaluates its condition, not because of a rule about cursors.
A single `FETCH NEXT` both retrieves the current row and advances. Counting rows is a separate job for `@@ROWCOUNT` or an aggregate query.
`FETCH NEXT` only moves forward. Reading backward needs a cursor declared `SCROLL` and an explicit `FETCH PRIOR`, neither of which appears here.
questions.takeaway: A T-SQL cursor loop needs a priming `FETCH` before `WHILE` and an advancing `FETCH` as the loop's final statement.

questions.scenarioTitle: Retiring the Nylon Dog Leash from the catalog
questions.stem: `DELETE_ITEM` is called with 'DG04', which invoice 50710 still lists as an ordered item. The body sits inside `BEGIN TRY` and `BEGIN CATCH`. What happens?
options: The item is deleted and invoice 50710 quietly loses the line that referred to it
The delete fails on the foreign key, and `CATCH` prints the message instead of crashing the caller
`@@ROWCOUNT` comes back as 1, because the `DELETE` matched a row before the constraint was checked
SQL Server removes the invoice line first and then the item, so the reference stays valid
optionNotes: A foreign key exists precisely to stop this. Allowing the delete would leave invoice line 50710 pointing at an item id that no longer exists.
Correct. The engine refuses the delete, control passes to `BEGIN CATCH`, and `ERROR_MESSAGE()` gives the caller a sentence instead of a raw engine error.
The statement never completes, so there is no successful row count to read. `@@ROWCOUNT` is the test for the different case where the item id simply was not in the table.
Cascading deletes happen only when the foreign key was declared `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Nothing here declares that, and silently deleting invoice lines would be a poor default anyway.
questions.takeaway: Wrap a delete in `TRY`/`CATCH` so a foreign key refusal becomes a readable message, and use `@@ROWCOUNT` for the separate case of a row that was never there.

questions.scenarioTitle: The grooming kit that lost four units
questions.stem: A clerk inserts one row into `INVOICE_LINE` for `GR15` with `NUM_ORDERED` of 4. Afterwards `ITEM.ON_HAND` for `GR15` reads 18 instead of 22. The `INSERT` statement mentions only `INVOICE_LINE`. What explains the change?
options: An `INSERT` automatically updates every table joined to the target by a foreign key
The engine recalculates `ON_HAND` from `INVOICE_LINE` each time `ITEM` is read
A `CHECK` constraint on `ITEM` adjusted the value to keep the two tables consistent
An `AFTER INSERT` trigger on `INVOICE_LINE` ran its own `UPDATE` against `ITEM`
optionNotes: A foreign key restricts what values are allowed; it never copies or adjusts data in the parent table. Nothing about `INSERT` propagates changes across a relationship.
`ON_HAND` is a stored column holding a number, not a computed one. Nothing recomputes it when the table is read.
A `CHECK` constraint can only accept or reject a value in the row being written. It cannot change a value, and it cannot touch a different table.
Correct. The trigger is attached to `INVOICE_LINE`, fires after the row lands, and issues an `UPDATE ITEM ... WHERE ITEM_ID = NEW.ITEM_ID` that no one reading the `INSERT` would ever see.
questions.takeaway: A trigger is the usual explanation when a table changes without any statement naming it, which is exactly why triggers must be documented.

questions.scenarioTitle: Harbor Pet Supply's oversized credit limit
questions.stem: KimTay wants a new customer row carrying a credit limit above 10000 refused outright, not written and then removed afterwards. Which trigger timing does that job?
options: `BEFORE INSERT`, which runs while the row is still a proposal and can cancel the statement
`AFTER INSERT`, because a row's values cannot be inspected until the row exists
`AFTER UPDATE`, since setting a credit limit is a change to a customer's terms
Either timing works, because a trigger can cancel a statement at any point
optionNotes: Correct. A `BEFORE` trigger runs before the row is stored, so raising an error there cancels the statement and nothing is ever written.
The proposed values are fully available to a `BEFORE` trigger through `NEW`. Waiting until after the row exists means writing it and then undoing it, which is what the requirement rules out.
The requirement is about a customer arriving for the first time, which is an insert. An update trigger would not fire at all on a new row.
Timing is exactly what differs. Cancelling from `AFTER` means the row was already written, and recovering from that is the transaction rollback problem the requirement was trying to avoid.
questions.takeaway: Use `BEFORE` for rules about whether a row may enter at all, and `AFTER` for consequences of a row that has already been accepted.

questions.scenarioTitle: Auditing a balance change at Access Pet Center
questions.stem: An `AFTER UPDATE OF BALANCE` trigger on `CUSTOMER` writes an audit row each time a balance moves. Which reference gives the balance as it stood before the `UPDATE`?
options: `NEW.BALANCE`, because the trigger body runs before the new value is applied
`OLD.BALANCE`, which holds the value the row carried when the `UPDATE` began
`BALANCE` on its own, because an unqualified column name always means the prior value
Neither, because an `AFTER` trigger runs too late to see a value that has been replaced
optionNotes: `NEW` always means the incoming version of the row. The timing word changes when the trigger runs, not which version each name refers to.
Correct. `OLD` is the row as it was and `NEW` is the row as it will be, which is what lets a single audit row record 3512.50 and 3762.50 side by side.
An unqualified column inside a trigger body is ambiguous at best and refers to whatever table the surrounding statement addresses. Audit code should always say `OLD.` or `NEW.` explicitly.
The whole purpose of `OLD` is to keep the previous version available to the trigger. It is present for updates and deletes and absent only for inserts.
questions.takeaway: `OLD` and `NEW` name the before and after versions of the row; an insert has no `OLD` and a delete has no `NEW`.

questions.scenarioTitle: Rebuilding KimTay's audit setup a second time
questions.stem: A sandbox box creates `INVOICE_LINE_LOG` and the trigger `LOG_NEW_LINE`, then inserts one invoice line. Why does the box open with `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS` and `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`?
options: Because a trigger stops working after it has fired once and has to be recreated
Because a `SELECT` cannot read a table that was created during an earlier run
Because the database survives between runs, so a second `CREATE` would fail on names that already exist
Because dropping the table is the only way to clear the rows the trigger wrote into it
optionNotes: A trigger fires every time its event happens, indefinitely. Nothing about firing consumes or disables it.
A table created in an earlier run is perfectly readable later; that persistence is the reason the drops are needed, not a reason they would not help.
Correct. The sandbox keeps its database from one press of Run to the next, so without the drops the second run fails on the existing table, the existing trigger, and the duplicate primary key.
`DELETE FROM INVOICE_LINE_LOG;` would empty it without dropping it. The table is dropped because the script recreates it, not because emptying it is impossible.
questions.takeaway: Any script you expect to run more than once should open with `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS` and `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` for everything it creates.

questions.scenarioTitle: The clinic with no invoice
questions.stem: KimTay wants a list of every customer alongside their invoice numbers, and Companion Care Clinic must appear even though it has no invoice at all. Which approach produces that?
options: An inner join between `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE`, which keeps every customer and shows zero for the missing invoice
A left outer join from `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE`, which keeps the clinic and shows null for its invoice number
An inner join with `WHERE INVOICE_NUM IS NULL` added, which brings the unmatched customer back into the result
A union of `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE`, which stacks the rows of both tables into a single list
optionNotes: An inner join keeps only rows that matched on both sides, so Companion Care Clinic is dropped entirely. It never invents a zero for a row it discarded.
Correct. A left outer join keeps every row of the left table whether or not it matched, filling the right table's columns with null when there was nothing to match.
The inner join has already removed the clinic before the `WHERE` clause runs, so there is no row left for `IS NULL` to find. This condition returns nothing at all.
`UNION` stacks results with matching column lists on top of each other. `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE` have different columns, and stacking would not pair a customer with its invoices anyway.
questions.takeaway: When a question says a row must appear even with nothing to match, it is asking for an outer join.

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay's categories with more than one item
questions.stem: `ITEM` holds five rows spread across four categories. Which clause narrows a grouped result down to only the categories holding more than one item?
options: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1`, placed immediately after the `FROM` clause
`ORDER BY COUNT(*) > 1`, which sorts the qualifying groups to the top of the result
`DISTINCT CATEGORY`, which removes the categories that appear only once
`HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, which is applied after `GROUP BY` has formed the groups
optionNotes: `WHERE` is evaluated row by row before any group exists, so `COUNT(*)` has nothing to count yet and the engine rejects the condition.
`ORDER BY` decides the order rows are returned in. It never removes a row, so every category would still be listed.
`DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from a result. It has no notion of how many rows went into each category and cannot filter on a count.

Correct. `HAVING` runs after `GROUP BY` has built the groups and their aggregate values, which is the only point at which `COUNT(*)` for a category is available to test. Only Habitat qualifies, with AV07 and FT88.
questions.takeaway: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after grouping, and only `HAVING` can test an aggregate.

questions.scenarioTitle: The clinic's missing invoice number
questions.stem: Nothing in KimTay's shipped data is missing, but a query can still produce a null. A left outer join from `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE` gives Companion Care Clinic a row whose `INVOICE_NUM` is null, because there was nothing on the right to match. Which condition keeps only the customers whose `INVOICE_NUM` came back null?
options: `WHERE I.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL`, because null is never equal to anything, including another null
`WHERE I.INVOICE_NUM = NULL`, which compares the column against the null value directly
`WHERE I.INVOICE_NUM = ''`, because a column with no value holds an empty string
`WHERE NOT I.INVOICE_NUM`, which is true whenever the column holds no value
optionNotes: Correct. Null means unknown, and a comparison with an unknown is itself unknown rather than true, so SQL provides `IS NULL` as the only way to test for it. Run it in the sandbox and exactly one row comes back: 1310, Companion Care Clinic.
This comparison evaluates to unknown for every row, including the null one, so the query returns nothing at all. It is the single most common null mistake.
An empty string is a known value of zero length; null is the absence of any value. An unmatched outer join column is null and does not match `= ''`.
`NOT` expects a condition, not a column. Even where an engine tolerates the syntax, a null operand makes the result unknown rather than true.
questions.takeaway: Test for a missing value with `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`; `= NULL` matches nothing, ever.

questions.scenarioTitle: Printing a rep's full name on a KimTay report
questions.stem: You need `LAST_NAME` and `FIRST_NAME` combined into one column, and the same statement has to work in MySQL and in this page's engine. Which expression does that?
options: `LAST_NAME + ', ' + FIRST_NAME`, since `+` joins text values in every SQL engine
`ADD(LAST_NAME, ', ', FIRST_NAME)`, the standard function for joining character values
`CONCAT(LAST_NAME, ', ', FIRST_NAME)`, which both engines accept with identical results
`JOIN LAST_NAME WITH FIRST_NAME`, the SQL keyword pair for combining two columns
optionNotes: `+` joins text in SQL Server but means numeric addition elsewhere, so the same expression gives a number, a null, or an error depending on the engine.
There is no `ADD` function in any of these engines. Addition is an operator, and it is arithmetic rather than text handling.
Correct. `CONCAT` behaves the same way in MySQL and SQLite, which is why it is the safe choice when a statement has to survive a change of engine. The `||` operator also works in both.
`JOIN` combines rows from two tables. It has nothing to do with combining two columns of one row into a single value.
questions.takeaway: `CONCAT` and `||` join text the same way in MySQL and SQLite; `+` is SQL Server's spelling and does not travel.

questions.scenarioTitle: Dating KimTay's audit rows
questions.stem: An audit trigger has to stamp each log row with the current date. Which pairing is correct for the two engines named?
options: `TODAY()` in MySQL and `TODAY()` in SQLite, since date handling is standardized across engines
`SYSDATE` in MySQL and `SYSDATE` in SQLite, which both resolve at the moment the row is written
`GETDATE()` in MySQL and `GETDATE()` in SQLite, the portable spelling of the current date
`CURDATE()` in MySQL and `DATE('now')` in SQLite, because the two engines spell it differently
optionNotes: `TODAY()` is not a function in either engine. Date handling is in fact where these engines diverge most, not where they agree.
`SYSDATE` is Oracle's spelling. MySQL has a `SYSDATE()` function with different behaviour from `CURDATE()`, and SQLite has nothing of the kind.
`GETDATE()` is SQL Server's spelling and is available in neither MySQL nor SQLite. There is no portable spelling of the current date across all four engines.
Correct. `CURDATE()`, `NOW()`, `YEAR()`, `DATEDIFF()` and `DATE_ADD()` are MySQL; SQLite uses `DATE('now')`, `strftime('%Y', col)`, `julianday(a) - julianday(b)` and `DATE(col, '+30 days')`.
questions.takeaway: Date functions are the least portable part of SQL; look up the spelling for the engine you are on every single time.

questions.scenarioTitle: One procedure for four KimTay customers
questions.stem: `GET_CUSTOMER` is written once but has to work for 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420. What makes a single stored procedure serve all four?
options: A view over `CUSTOMER` that the procedure reads instead of reading the table directly
An input parameter, supplied by the caller each time the procedure is executed
A cursor, which is the only mechanism that lets a procedure see more than one customer
A separately stored copy of the procedure for each customer number in the table
optionNotes: A view is a stored query with a fixed definition. It does not accept a value from the caller, so it cannot change which customer is returned from one call to the next.
Correct. The parameter is substituted into the `WHERE` clause on every execution, which is exactly what makes one stored routine reusable instead of single-purpose.
A cursor is about processing many rows one at a time. This procedure deliberately handles a single row; the varying part is which row, and that is the parameter's job.
Storing one procedure per customer would mean a new procedure every time KimTay signs a customer. Parameters exist precisely so that never has to happen.
questions.takeaway: A parameter is what turns stored code from a single-purpose script into something worth storing.

questions.scenarioTitle: Handling one rep's customers one at a time
questions.stem: A single `SELECT` already returns both of rep 20's customers in one result. Why would a procedure use a cursor over that query instead?
options: A cursor is faster than a `SELECT` because it loads the whole table into memory first
A `SELECT` may not include a `WHERE` clause once it is written inside a stored procedure
A cursor lets the procedure run its own logic once per row, one row at a time
A cursor is required whenever a query returns more than one column of data
optionNotes: A cursor is generally slower, because the engine gives up set-based optimisation and hands rows over one at a time. Speed is a reason to avoid cursors, not to choose them.
A `SELECT` inside a procedure is an ordinary `SELECT` with every clause available. Nothing about being stored restricts the query.
Correct. The cursor exists so that code can run between rows, making a decision or performing an action per row that a single statement could not express.
Column count has nothing to do with it. A one-column query can drive a cursor and a twenty-column query can be returned as an ordinary result set.
questions.takeaway: Choose a cursor only when each row needs its own decision; when a single statement can answer the question, it is both shorter and faster.

questions.scenarioTitle: A customer number that is not on file
questions.stem: In Oracle, a `SELECT ... INTO` inside a procedure matches no row. What happens immediately afterwards?
options: `NO_DATA_FOUND` is raised, and the `EXCEPTION` section decides what the caller is told
The procedure returns an empty result set to the caller and finishes normally
The target variables are left unchanged and execution continues with the next statement
Oracle re-runs the query without its `WHERE` clause so the variables receive some value
optionNotes: Correct. `SELECT ... INTO` promises exactly one row, so zero rows is a failure with a name, and control jumps to the handlers you wrote.
A procedure using `SELECT ... INTO` is not producing a result set at all; it is filling variables. There is no empty result to hand back.
This describes what MySQL does when no `NOT FOUND` handler was declared. Oracle deliberately refuses to continue on values that were never retrieved.
No engine silently broadens a query you wrote. Returning an arbitrary customer instead of the requested one would be far worse than raising an error.
questions.takeaway: Oracle names its two single-row failures and expects a handler; silence is not one of the options.

questions.scenarioTitle: An update at KimTay that changed nothing
questions.stem: A T-SQL procedure updates `CUSTOMER` using a customer number that is not in the table. How does the procedure find out that no row changed?
options: It reads `@@FETCH_STATUS`, which reports a non-zero value when an `UPDATE` matches nothing
It waits for SQL Server to raise an error, because an `UPDATE` matching no row always fails
It counts the table's rows before and after the statement inside a cursor loop
It tests `@@ROWCOUNT` on the statement immediately after the `UPDATE` and finds it is 0
optionNotes: `@@FETCH_STATUS` reports on the most recent cursor `FETCH`. It has nothing to say about an `UPDATE` and would hold a stale value here.
An `UPDATE` that matches no row is a complete success that happened to affect nothing. SQL Server raises no error, which is exactly why the check is needed.
The row count of `CUSTOMER` does not change when an `UPDATE` matches nothing, and it does not change when an `UPDATE` succeeds either. A cursor adds work without adding information.
Correct. `@@ROWCOUNT` holds the number of rows the preceding statement affected, and every following statement overwrites it, so it must be read straight away and saved if it is needed twice.
questions.takeaway: `@@ROWCOUNT` is T-SQL's answer to "did that actually do anything", and it must be read on the very next statement.

questions.scenarioTitle: Keeping KimTay's stock figures honest
questions.stem: Every new row in `INVOICE_LINE` must reduce `ITEM.ON_HAND` by the quantity ordered, and nobody wants to depend on each programmer remembering to write the second statement. What handles this?
options: A `CHECK` constraint on `ITEM`, which recalculates `ON_HAND` whenever it would be violated
An `AFTER INSERT` trigger on `INVOICE_LINE` that issues the `UPDATE` against `ITEM`
A view joining `ITEM` to `INVOICE_LINE` so that `ON_HAND` is always current when read
An index on `INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID`, which keeps the two tables synchronized as rows arrive
optionNotes: A `CHECK` constraint accepts or rejects a value in the row being written. It cannot change a value and it cannot reach into a different table.
Correct. The trigger is attached to `INVOICE_LINE`, fires once per inserted row, and runs the `UPDATE` no matter which program did the insert or whether its author knew the rule existed.
A view is a stored query. Reading it can compute a current figure, but it cannot change the stored `ON_HAND` column that the rest of the system reads.
An index affects how quickly rows are located. It stores no logic and changes no data, so it cannot enforce a rule of any kind.
questions.takeaway: A rule that must hold no matter who writes the statement belongs in the database, and a trigger is the tool when a constraint cannot express it.

matchers.heading: Match the Requirement to the Trigger
matchers.prompt: Each card below states something KimTay or StayWell wants the database to do. Decide which trigger timing does that job, or whether a trigger is the wrong tool entirely. Every card belongs in exactly one zone.

zones.label: BEFORE INSERT
zones.hint: Refuse a row before it is stored

zones.label: AFTER INSERT
zones.hint: Act on a row already accepted

zones.label: AFTER UPDATE
zones.hint: Record a change that has happened

cards.text: Refuse a new customer row whose credit limit is above the approval ceiling
cards.why: The row must never be stored at all, and only a BEFORE trigger runs while the statement can still be cancelled.

cards.text: Reject a room that arrives with a negative monthly rent
cards.why: This is a rule about whether the row may enter, decided from NEW before anything is written.

cards.text: Subtract the quantity ordered from ITEM.ON_HAND once the invoice line exists
cards.why: The stock adjustment is a consequence of a line that has already been accepted, so it belongs after the row is on file.

cards.text: Copy every new invoice line into an audit table together with the date
cards.why: An audit row should record what was actually stored, which is only certain once the insert has succeeded.

cards.text: Store the previous balance and the new balance side by side for auditors
cards.why: Only an update has both OLD and NEW, and the pair is written after the change has been applied.

cards.text: Note in a log which room's rent changed and by how much
cards.why: The entry is computed from OLD and NEW on an existing row, which is the update case, recorded after the fact.

cards.text: Speed up lookups of KimTay customers by their rep number
cards.why: Making a query faster is what an index does; a trigger stores logic, not an access path.

cards.text: Guarantee a customer's rep number matches a rep that actually exists
cards.why: A foreign key constraint enforces this declaratively, and a constraint should always be preferred over a trigger that does the same job.

matchers.heading: Match the Term to Its Engine
matchers.prompt: Each card names something from this module. Sort it into the dialect it belongs to, or into the last zone if the idea is shared by MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server alike. Every card fits exactly one zone.

cards.text: %TYPE, which borrows a column's declared data type for a variable
cards.why: Only Oracle offers this anchoring; MySQL and SQL Server require you to restate the type by hand.

cards.text: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR, returning a numbered message between -20000 and -20999
cards.why: That numbering scheme and function name exist only in Oracle.

cards.text: @@FETCH_STATUS, tested to decide whether a cursor loop continues
cards.why: This is SQL Server's global fetch indicator; Oracle uses the cursor's own %NOTFOUND attribute.

cards.text: DEALLOCATE, which releases a cursor's name so it can be declared again
cards.why: Only SQL Server separates closing a cursor from freeing its name.

cards.text: The inserted table, holding every row a statement added
cards.why: SQL Server triggers fire once per statement and read affected rows from inserted and deleted rather than from NEW.

cards.text: DELIMITER //, which stops the client splitting the routine at each semicolon
cards.why: This is a MySQL client instruction; Oracle ends a block with a slash and SQL Server uses GO.

cards.text: A cursor that is declared, opened, fetched from in a loop, and closed
cards.why: All three engines provide cursors with the same four-stage lifecycle, differing only in how the loop is written.

cards.text: A stored procedure that takes a parameter and is run on request
cards.why: Named, parameterised, stored logic is common to MySQL, Oracle and SQL Server; only the header syntax changes.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE REP_CUSTOMER_LIST (I_REP_NUM IN CHAR) AS
BEGIN

CREATE TRIGGER REDUCE_ON_HAND
ON INVOICE_LINE
AFTER INSERT
AS
UPDATE ITEM
SET    ON_HAND = ITEM.ON_HAND - T.QTY
FROM   ITEM
       JOIN (SELECT ITEM_ID, SUM(NUM_ORDERED) AS QTY
             FROM   inserted
             GROUP BY ITEM_ID) T
         ON ITEM.ITEM_ID = T.ITEM_ID;
GO
